utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please be seated. Registrar, would you have the accused brought in, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning to the interpreters. I'm sure that everything is functioning properly since there was a hearing before this one, which also explains why we have encountered some delay now. I, first of all, would like to say good morning to all of the parties present, Office of the Prosecutor, and to the Defence, to the accused and then begin our final day. I see Mr. Greaves has changed his seat. I hope that he slept well. Have you slept well, Mr. Greaves? Perhaps the final argument will be shorter than he originally said, but I'm only joking. Take all the time that you need, Mr. Greaves. Take as long as you need, Mr. Greaves. We can begin. I think if we can, if we can finish with the Prosecutor's final argument this morning, we will. We'll take a break at 11.30, because the interpreters are tired; they began working this morning, and the Judges may be a bit tired as well, even though, of course, the Judges are never tired, indefatigable. I see Mr. Greaves is still standing. Did you want to say something, Mr. Greaves?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I was looking at the transcript. I haven't got my earphones on and I thought it was going to be something that required me to say something, but I won't say anything at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, not at all. I'm trying to make a joke. I'm trying to reach the level of British humour, which is legendary, but I don't think I'm able to do that. In any case, without any further ado, I suppose that Mr. Nice -- good morning -- who is going to begin his final argument. I give you the floor, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. There was, I think, going to be documents my learned friend wished to put in. We had one document that was going to be submitted in addition. I don't think he wants our document to go in, but I don't object to his documents going in if he wants them in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. I thought there was just the report of the detention unit commander that had been asked for. The Defence received it late. But you received it today; is that correct, Mr. Greaves? It's on the Judges' desk here in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I'm grateful for Your Honours' indicating that you now have the report of Mr. McFadden. Your Honour, there are some documents which we would wish to submit, and the reason you hadn't heard about them until now is because they were the subject of discussions between my learned friend and myself, and we had not yet reached any position as to agreement or otherwise. May I, therefore, submit a total of seven folders which contain English translations and some originals or copies of originals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. As far as the document which the Prosecution indicated that they would wish to present, as far as the Defence is concerned, we do not accept the truth or the contents they have thereof, and I indicate that in advance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What document are you speaking about, Mr. Greaves?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: The document that Your Honour has just been told by my learned friend he would wish to present in due course a moment or two ago. That's what my learned friend --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. I need some help here because I don't really understand. I thought that we would begin with the final arguments this morning. Mr. Tochilovsky, what document are you talking about? What is being contested? What truth is being contested? Can you tell us, please, so if we need to take a decision we will.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: It's mostly about the Defence documents, the documents the Defence wants to be admitted. As it was mentioned already that the Prosecution in general doesn't object to the admission of these documents, but we have just a few comments on that. First of all, about the credibility of those documents that the Defence just produced to the Judges, to the new panel, for instance, there are two letters of discharge from the medical centre in Brcko of the accused. According to one letter, the accused was treated in that centre from 8 September to 9 September, 1992, and he was admitted with a wound in the left foot. According to another letter of discharge from the same hospital, on the same dates, 8 September to 15 September, he was treated for firearm wounds in the right shank, in the right ankle joint. So these documents apparently contradict each other. It's about the credibility of those documents. Another point is that the other documents the Defence presented has the certificate of 17 June, 1998, according to which Goran Jelisic served in the army of Republika Srpska from 28 June, 1992 to 20 April, 1996. At the same time, the Defence asked to admit the case history, according to which Goran Jelisic was employed by the Ministry of the Interior, MUP, the 30th of July, 1992. With regard to the document which was mentioned, the document the Prosecution would like to be admitted alongside with the documents of the Defence. The Defence produced the case history and findings, according to which the accused was examined -- was examined on his psychological status on 31st July, 1992, and according to this report, he may have elements of paranoia. At the end of this document, it says that it is necessary for him to undergo psychiatric examination and treatment in a psychiatric clinic in Belgrade. Of course, it is helpful for the Judges to see the report on psychological studies of the accused from Belgrade. It is logical. The Defence did not produce that document. The Prosecution has the document. We have the document from Belgrade, and according to that document, Goran was admitted to the Belgrade clinic on 31st July. He was there from the 31st to the 3rd of August, 1992, and from that document it's clear that psychologically there is no evidence, according to that document, no evident signs of disturbance in thinking and perception, critical thinking and consideration was preserved. Maybe this is why the Defence doesn't want this document to be admitted. But without this document, the documents that the Defence wants to be admitted, those documents don't give the whole picture of what was going on at that time. So this is a few points on the documents that the Defence wants to be admitted. Again, in general, the Prosecution has no objection to the admission of those documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Mr. Greaves, Mr. Tochilovsky, I will consult with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Judges will take all of the documents and will evaluate the relevance of those documents after they've heard the final arguments. Mr. Prosecutor, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It is of course a privilege and an education to appear in an International Tribunal with Judges from around the world, and before I start what I want to say about the defendant, I must record that in prosecuting this case, a large number of lawyers and investigators have been involved, not full time on this case but the Chamber will recall Mr. Terree Bowers opened the case about a year ago; that in the conduct of the case, he and I have been assisted throughout by Mr. Tochilovsky, the very senior legal advisor who has been with me throughout. We've had assistance from Mr. Bergsmo, who has been in court from time to time in the drafting and preparation of legal argument, the indefatigable assistance of Ms. Bauer, who sits in Court today, my legal officer, and who has done a range of tasks on this important case. Then there's been the investigators of whom you're heard, Mr. O'Donnell and Mr. Basham, who gave evidence. Finally, there have been two case managers, Ms. Javier-Annink and Ms. Reynders, who sits with me, who have never missed a document or, I think, failed to meet a deadline. They being assisted by somebody you've never seen but who produces the documents, again working very hard, Ms. Walpita. Sometimes, from time to time, interns working free at this institution, such as a Mr. Duhaime, recently have added their shoulder to the wheel. So it's a privilege to work with such people. At the end of the exercise I take full responsibility, of course, for what happens, especially if anything goes wrong or if I say anything that is incorrect, but, nevertheless, insofar as the case is a success, it is a team job. In presenting our closing arguments to you, I'm going to distribute two documents, each of which I hope will take far less time to deal with than their initial appearance might suggest. The first document is my argument. I regret that it is not in French. It was only concluded, as the Chamber might expect, this morning. I am very mindful of the need to speak at a speed that accommodates the needs both of the interpreters and the English and French stenographers, and if anyone has difficulty, because sometimes I speak too fast, I hope that they will draw it to my attention and I will immediately slow down. I have French at my neck in the hope that an injunction that I should do something different will be heard by me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You can count on me, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This man, Goran Jelisic, was not just a willing executioner. He killed in unquestioning and happy obedience to any instruction to kill, however minimally expressed. He killed as if for pleasure on his own initiative or on a whim. He has never given a satisfactory or even a consistent account of how he became involved, how he was trusted to kill and kill and kill again. He claims to have acted on orders, but the Chamber will no doubt be alive to the possibility that he was, in truth, a volunteer. If he was such a volunteer, or indeed even if he is shown never to have told the truth about how he became involved, so much the worse for him. Recent discussion about borderline personalities cannot obscure the fact that civilised societies operate criminal justice systems on the basis that people bear responsibility for their acts, unless their mental state falls below a line normally associated with severe mental illness. Although personality disorders may, in certain regimes or systems, change the circumstances in which a convicted person is held, sometimes keeping them longer in mental institutions than they would be in prison, there is no suggestion here that this defendant qualifies for such special treatment. He falls to be dealt with, as would the leaders of this or of other wars of terror who themselves probably had or have personality disorders, as a man of full age and responsibility. Every human instinct, we respectfully suggest -- whether in the bereaved, in such victims this man has survived, or indeed even in the hearts and minds of lawyers and judges -- will be that this man should receive the maximum possible sentence and should never again breathe the air of free society. But before galvanising such instincts into judgement, this Chamber has to consider whether there are factors that properly mitigate the natural view and that must be taken into account to reduce, inevitably at most to a modest extent, that maximum sentence. At first sight, there are some such factors: the defendant's behaviour, as the Defence will argue, before and after the killings as reflecting some essential good, his confessions, cooperation, and the pleas of guilty. But as listed, these are only at first sight, and the fact that this is a sentencing exercise or part of the trial cannot free the Chamber from rigorous analysis of all the material and from the duty owed to itself, to the International Community, and to the victims to explore these factors in depth. If, on analysis, they or some of them are, in truth, further cynical reflections of the same wicked or corrupted mind that dispatched so many innocent Bosnian Muslims to wretched death, then it would be wrong to accord him benefit, unless the jurisprudence is clear that practical benefits, however arising, do buy a benefit. The Prosecution questions each of these potential mitigating factors, and I turn first to the Defence evidence, essentially, of his behaviour. To what extent was the defendant's behaviour, given by Defence witnesses, driven by knowledge that he would one day have to face these very accusations against which he prepared a smoke screen? To what extent have the Defence witnesses misled you by repeated assertions that they were told only that he was forced to kill, never taking natural inquiry further? Where Defence witnesses spoke of the defendant as a good, young boy without discriminative tendencies, the Chamber will have in mind that this is probably of no relevance, given that all ethnic groups in Bijeljina, a predominantly Muslim town, got on well before the war. It is the corrupting of those good relations that is, in part, the real evil of the war of which we hear so much in this Tribunal. Witnesses such as DL, DO, and DS had only occasional contact with this man and showed lack of knowledge of things upon which he relied, like his relations with his family, his jealousy of his sister, and so on. Closer friends were uninformed of the real circumstances of his life; DJ apparently ignorant of his criminal activities; his best friend, DM, counting him a coward, knowing of his criminal activities, and spending the stolen money with him is a witness of whom the Chamber will inevitably be cautious. Although in light of the psychiatric evidence yesterday, it's interesting to note that DM pointed out the defendant liked money and it was greed that led to crime, nothing else. Witness DR, whose son was taken on holiday, showed huge trust for no apparent reason. Was this her naivety in the face of the defendant's naivety? Was it naivety in the face of a false story by the defendant? Is the story itself true or false? None of the supposed possible or intended victims at Luka, allegedly spared by the defendant, have been called to testify, and stories coming through third parties, which I list in paragraph 13 or I identify, come from witnesses who are alive and well and should have been here themselves. All this evidence, carefully assessed, fits with the defendant's delusion of grandeur and narcissistic tendency. It shows neither remorse, nor contrition but are other facets of the same personality that committed these crimes. Setting up of mitigation witnesses fits with manipulation. Helping Muslims, if he did, fits with his wanting to be seen as a hero, not an executioner, and the Chamber may conclude he did not do these favours out of remorse or guilt but to polish his ego, and they cannot benefit him. Strangely, paragraph 16, almost none of the witnesses dealt with his behaviour between Brcko and his arrest, none of them speaking of his qualities as a family man, less still as a worker, and it is something of a mystery, what happened in that period of time, although it's clear that residents in his town must have known of what he was reported to have done. One witness spoke of 1997, that was DO, the joint holiday he organised. By then, the defendant knew he was indicted and was hunted, and that witness's reliability has to be set against his finding of refuge for a known indictee of this Tribunal and doing so with a false name. The witness called this week, DQ, given evidence of the hunted, or was it the haunted, man thinking of surrender shows this defendant seeking to pursue his own interests and, to some degree, his family's when he asked for 50.000 dollars in difficult and increasingly impossible circumstances. But his ease of contact with such a public figure as DQ in public places raises the issue of whether his movements were known and even supervised in a town where he could move freely. His ability to have a false identification card at his arrest but apparently to show his real card to the Witness DQ is, similarly, odd. At the end of DQ's evidence, the fact is that the defendant could easily have surrendered. He actually tried to effect some advantage for himself and he did not surrender. Consistent with that evidence, the other Defence evidence shows that during the wartime and thereafter, the defendant could move freely in Bijeljina and Brcko, that he had money to give away, maybe from smuggling as he, I think, says in his interview, and the Chamber may conclude that he wasn't in such great danger, at least not initially, of being liquidated by the authority of Bijeljina or Brcko and that he did not, in truth, have to hide from anyone, at least at most times. We conclude by inviting the Chamber to say that the witnesses presented on his behalf established nothing to constitute material mitigation. Some fall to be discounted for having given evidence by videolink without good cause. If the Prosecution evidence showing enthusiasm to kill is accepted, then all that evidence from Defence witnesses suggesting reluctance to kill is unreliable. Either it is to be distrusted or it reveals the defendant having a mind capable of being split into highly contradictory behaviour or patterns, apparently at the same time. But it is always possible that a borderline personality, creating its own reality, as the psychiatrists told us yesterday, has lied about events to some or all of these witnesses and, therefore, lies through them to this Court. The developing picture of the defendant, built on his lay witnesses and on his psychiatrist's evidence, may be contrasted with what we untutored, non-experts, as of course we all are, might nevertheless imagine a truly remorseful and contrite person would show. Where, we ask, is the agony of reflecting on the heads, the faces, and the bodies of those he killed, the agony of the guilt to their families? Where, indeed, does he say anything spontaneous and from the heart to show a moment's care, except for himself? He took advantage of a war situation to embark on some form of self-gratification by the exercise of all and the ultimate control. Does such a man, we ask, have the right to enjoy freedom again, and would justice be served if he did? The Chamber should know that the weight of the document I've handed in includes an annex at the end, to which I will pay no further attention but which occupies pages 31 to the end and which is a fuller analysis of the Defence witnesses' evidence. It's available for reference should that be of assistance. I turn, on page 8, to the defendant's confessions in interview. To what extent were those admissions sanitised versions of a grimmer reality? They were only made after the service of statements that showed the impossible task he had of denying the killings he eventually admitted. Were they made not to reflect anguish and contrition but to mislead this Chamber into finding him less evil than, in reality, he was? The Chamber will note, on analysis, the limited degree to which he went beyond what was proved to the hilt in the papers served and, indeed, his refusal to allow certain topics to be explored, including, as we know, the whole issue of genocide, the charge now acquitted for lack of evidence state of mind. I will deal with those interviews more fully when we look at the evidence generally. I turn to cooperation. The defendant's cooperation with the Prosecution has not been substantial and ongoing. The Chamber will see throughout my address footnote references. I don't propose to read any of them out, unless it's thought essential that I should do so, but they either identify support for propositions I advance in the text or they identify relevant passages of the evidence in the case. If it has not been substantial and ongoing, maybe it should not be considered as a mitigating factor in the sentencing. To be considered substantial, the cooperation extended to the Prosecutor must be significant and must contribute in a meaningful way to the administration of justice, but I observe that this is supported by a presentencing brief, not by a judgement, in the Kambanda case, although it doesn't appear that it was disagreed with. Several factors show that the defendant's cooperation was not significant and did not contribute in a meaningful way. It did not contribute to the effective arrest of other defendants or to the effective pursuit of other suspects or targets, and it did not lead to significant investigations. The defendant did not surrender himself voluntarily. The information provided was not considered by the Prosecution as useful, taking into consideration the fact that it was mainly public information or information of common knowledge, except with respect to his own acts. The Prosecution considers part of the information to be unreliable or incorrect because of inconsistencies and because of the sanitised version of events given. It is right to note, as I do at the end of subparagraph (c), he did make, as the Chamber will recall, specific allegations -- and I believe the name was in private session and, therefore, it doesn't appear here -- but he made specific allegations about a member of a body, which I have identified in the text, and indeed blamed that person fully for what he says he was ordered to do. Further, cooperation was limited because the defendant, as indeed the psychiatrist reminded us yesterday, was very definite about that which he was and that which he was not prepared to discuss. There was no plea agreement between the Prosecution and the defendant confirming significant cooperation in this case, and in the upshot, the Prosecution did not and does not invite the Trial Chamber to consider the cooperation as a significant mitigating factor. Pleas of guilty. To what extent do the pleas of guilty justify a reduction of the otherwise appropriate sentence? Given the nature of the evidence served and the circumstances in which the pleas were tendered, we argue that they should not be considered as a significant mitigating factor. Such pleas being considered as such factors only in specific circumstances. Sometimes a guilty plea is an indicator of remorse, but the Chamber may conclude that there is no evidence of genuine remorse here. And the Prosecution respectfully submits that the Trial Chamber should consider the remorse related evidence of the Defence as particularly unreliable. Again, I digress perhaps in the text as in what I say, but we were reminded yesterday that the first and only time of anything approaching tears of remorse came in that very last psychiatric examination prepared for these purposes or for the purposes of evidence and with all the benefit of the previous psychiatric and psychological reports at his hand. The defendant is never found breaking down at the image of someone he's killed, or with shame, guilt, or grief, thinking of the bereaved, of the unborn families, and so on. I turn to paragraph 28. A guilty plea, sparing the victims the need to testify or to wait -- I'm sorry, something has gone wrong there -- to testify could be considered as a mitigating factor. But as has been revealed, there has been significant cross-examination of many of the witnesses. Even had there been in trial on genocide, much of the same evidence would inevitably have to be adduced to prove the facts of the plea, given that the defendant showed by his cross-examination that he did not accept the witness statements and that would have led inevitably to the need to resolve contested issues of fact by witnesses called for sentencing purposes. So that the guilty pleas tendered have not had the effect of sparing all the witnesses from giving evidence. A guilty plea should not necessarily be considered as significant mitigation where prior to the plea the defendant is given access to evidence that shows he has little choice. In such circumstances, the plea may appear little more than a tactical manoeuvre to obtain a lighter sentence or some other advantage. Particularly important, again, where no remorse is revealed. In this case, the defendant consulted the evidence prior to interview. He admitted little beyond what was shown in the evidence. Some killings, it's true, a few, but not very much. The Chamber will be aware of the degree to which witnesses were able to speak, sometimes in detail and sometimes in only general terms, of numerous other killings by this defendant, far in excess of what was articulated with precision and thus what was admitted. I repeat. The defendant was concerned with psychiatrists and with the investigators to set the agenda for interviews and to exclude topics. That reality serves two purposes; one his and one the Chamber's. He avoided questions that may have been crucial and difficult, and provided unmistakable evidence of his need and desire to control, supporting the psychiatric opinion, boding not well to his future, but also supporting our proposition that the pleas of guilty bring him little credit or none because they were not, the Chamber may conclude, in any sense a full admission. If regardless of these points the Trial Chamber was to consider the defendant's guilty plea a mitigating factor, we submit that the extensive evidence of aggravating factors referred to later overrides any possible mitigating force of the plea. A guilty plea can be, but in this case is not, of importance to national reconciliation. By way of coda to our submissions, we also observe that the defendant's conduct in trial may undermine the benefit of his pleas. One has to be generous of human frailty, of course of real illness, even in those on trial, even in those who are wicked, but the Chamber and indeed the Prosecution has, of course, observed some of the behaviour of this defendant, and the Prosecution asks the Chamber whether he has been playing straight and fair with the Chamber and with the witnesses for whom the giving of evidence is an important event in the restructuring of their lives. And if he hasn't been playing fair, that is not to his credit but it has to be said, to his discredit. I turn to another topic and notice the time on the clock.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I was going to suggest that to you, since you've finished a part of your final argument. We are going to adjourn for 15 to 20 minutes. The Court stands adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can resume the hearing now. Have the accused brought in, please. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nice, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I turn, on page 12 of the note, to the background which must be sketched in. What is the relevant background for a man guilty of crime in time of war? Principally it is the man himself. He is his own background and he can draw little or no comfort from the wider background of war against which it must be remembered some suffer as victims, some behave innocently, some behave nobly. Probably the most helpful material for the Chamber will be the psychiatric and psychological reports, although, of course, they proceed on the basis of what the man himself says. To an extent they may, therefore, be the self-serving accounts of the man and they may be unreliable, those accounts to the psychiatrists, if he has misled them. Each conceded that as a possibility. Nevertheless, clear patterns emerge. As a man, he blamed everyone for his shortcomings; parents, sister. He blamed the sight of his dead grandmother, his grandparents for spoiling him or for making him uneasy. He blamed alcohol, drugs, bad company, the forced separation from his first wife, in a startling passage in that first interview. He blamed pre-detention in Tuzla, where problems of ethnic or problems with ethnic groups started. He even blamed his young wife for tricking him into marriage, and the Serbian police for threatening to take his children away as the reason for him staying silent. He bragged particularly about women, and I've set out the passages. He was unable to display discipline, he avoided taking responsibility whether in the army or elsewhere, yet viewed himself in glowing terms as sensitive, with a pure spirit, good and never bad, of high moral and emotional standards, a person who was having a positive effect, he says, on the people in Yugoslavia. He was a person and is a person who has lied to the very experts upon whom he depends and to some degree still relies. Spectacularly about being tortured in Croatia, and the Trial Chamber will recall the details to which he went; veins cut, hot coals, hit by concrete bars, then saying he was recaptured by Serbs who tortured him by salting his wounds. All of that, now the subject of a request to rub it out completely, although of course, the Defence would seek to distinguish between Croatian torture and Serbian torture. But in fact, one has to look more widely at the evidence to see what an accomplished and forward-thinking liar this man has been. Yesterday, I think, the Chamber, in some of its questions, understandably was allowing for the possibility, as he claims, that his lawyers had forced him to make up this account. When I say "allowing for that possibility," the Chamber, acting fairly, would be bound to do so, to allow the possibility. A year ago, Witness A, and more recently Witness DH, produced evidence that this man was complaining of Croatian torture in 1992. So it simply isn't possible that the lawyers compelled him to make it up. And one witness called on his own behalf. It was a story he was peddling shortly after his time at Brcko. He showed a scar. And when the Defence seek to partition off the Serbian torture, which was the salt-in-the-wound torture, that was also spoken of in 1992. So it may well be all the material about torture is a complete fraud. I turn over to page 15. He obviously lied to someone, either Van den Bussche or Dr. Duits, about things that he claimed in one report had been written down incorrectly. He's a man who claims to have done good at Luka with the priest and with the Imam. He claims disturbance following what he was forced to do, dreams; anxiety; depression; and, finally, tears. He is found by the experts to be a person who was justifying his actions, incapable of putting himself in another's shoes, manipulative, needing a father figure, egocentric and with delusions of grandeur, creating his own reality, yet once and only once, according to Van den Bussche, having remorse. He is seen as a man intense and on a mission to show the world that he's ready to do penance, but as Dr. Duits says, he turns everything around and glorifies in his full cooperation, unaware of how he is inverting reality. He is diagnosed as showing a personality disorder with antisocial tendencies, a behavioural problem characteristic by narcissistic, antisocial, and avoidance tendencies, of but of course that psychiatrist was still working on the basis of torture, saying, as the Chamber may recall, that he had post-traumatic stress disorder, but as I say at the top of page 16, not to the extent one would expect given the traumatic experiences. The defendant was almost caught out there and then by those careful psychiatrists examining him. Diagnosis showing no remorse, little emotion with no deep feeling of regret, according to Dr. Herfst, and although this was challenged by the defendant, the Chamber will have to form its own view and may conclude that there is no ability and no reality in -- there is no ability to show and there is no reality in remorse. I quite understand and sympathise with the difficulties that the Defence are placed in by the ruling that's applied to them from the Registry about Dr. Petkovic, but my duty remains to rely upon it -- my duty remains to remind the Chamber that the view of the person with the greatest contact with this man was that he could not control aggressive impulses. This was the reason for his behaviour in war; that he was primitive and unable to defer to his needs. A serious personality disorder was diagnosed, and he was found to have an angry charge related to his paranoid undercurrent, culminating in a clearly malicious, strongly paranoid rejection of people previously idealised. Well, Your Honours have had the psychiatric evidence recently. It will be fresh in your mind. There is an agreement really about the personality; there's agreement about the ability to be deceased; there's agreement about the manipulation. The examination even suggesting remorse, raised it only in relation -- I beg your pardon, raised tears not in relation to the victims but in relation to his contemplating those witnesses coming on his own behalf. So that's the background of the man. It's not pleasant to have to sketch these things out in such detail, even for a man facing sentencing for these crimes, but it has to be done in order that a fair appraisal of him and his responsibility can be made. Of course, to the psychiatrists, but also to the investigators, he claims that he was only acting on orders, and so I turn briefly, before looking at aggravating circumstances, to the issue of superior orders as an element to be considered within the mitigation evidence that's been called, and generally. The fact that the defendant was not the commander of the Luka camp or a higher Bosnian Serb official should not be considered as a mitigating factor. The Nuremberg jurisprudence clearly shows that the fact that a defendant was a low-level perpetrator did not prevent imposition of the most severe sentences. In the Essen Lynching Case, a civilian was sentenced to death for the killing of a prisoner of war, while a private soldier went to life imprisonment for having failed to interfere with a crowd that had murdered prisoners entrusted with their custody. In the Belsen Case, four officials in Belsen and Auschwitz concentration camps were sentenced to death. A prisoner appointed camp senior in Belsen went to life imprisonment. In the Trial of Peter Bach, a German civilian was sentenced to death for killing a prisoner, and in the Trial of Karl Buck and Ten Others, people in charge of a camp and two guards were sentenced to death for killing prisoners of war and civilians. Finally, in the Hadmar Case, the defendants were staff members of a small sanatorium in Germany and three were sentenced to death, four to prison terms ranging from 25 years to life. All of these defendants could claim for mitigation of superior orders. It availed them nothing. There is no intervening glass ceiling, to borrow a modern analogy, I think, from the business world, but there is no glass ceiling that separates for sentencing purposes those who are further down the chain of responsibility from those who are at the top. I turn to aggravating circumstances, as I think it is my duty to do, and suggest to the Chamber, at the top of page 18, paragraph 37, that aggravating circumstances in the following categories may be revealed: Dishonesty; enthusiasm to threaten, abuse, show ethnic hatred, and humiliate his victims, in short, discriminatory behaviour of a high order; the enthusiasm to exercise power, ultimately to kill even for pleasure; and the susceptibility to authority figures, for man is assumed able to question and resist the evil of others. I'll approach the material by categories or by topics, again observing that if the defendant is revealed not to have been accurate or honest in his account, to have attempted to obscure in relation to any of these topics, that does him no good and may itself be an aggravating circumstance. Paragraph 39. Of course, personality problems that may not be attractive but which pre-exist crime cannot amount to aggravation. On the contrary, the Chamber is invited to say that the man must be accepted for what he was, even though that weakness of personality may not constitute mitigation. There is lack of clarity as to what he did between 1988 and 1990; maybe there were things he wished to hide. He began forging cheques in 1990. His sentence of three years and seven months was followed by events for which there is no great clarity in the accounts before the Chamber. I set them out on page 19, I've covered them with the experts yesterday, and I save time by going to page 20. We turn to the recruitment and to the killings themselves. The Chamber will recall what Dr. Herfst said about how easily he could identify with people in authority, how, if placed in a position of power, he will unconsciously view this as a confirmation and reinforcement of his identity and experience feelings of his own worth. The Chamber will probably recall what Dr. Duits said yesterday about the saying of giving someone a gun and a Motorola and he is God. It appears, from all the material, that he learnt about the plan to reinforce the Serbs in Brcko at a funeral, may have been recruited, went to Brcko, meeting a named person, paragraph 46, being told about the plan to blow the bridges and about the start of the war. In his account to psychiatrists and psychologists, he explains how he was put under pressure by paramilitary groups, wanted to run away but was given the name Adolf in circumstances where obedience was demanded. He blamed radicals to Dr. Herfst. On the top of page 21, he told that same doctor that he was summoned and ordered to kill Muslims, called Adolf, as told he had to kill and given a list, and that he would be killed if he did not kill, was provided with alcohol and pills. Dr. Duits, at the end of April, he said he was approached and ordered to report in uniform, otherwise he would be killed, and he then went on to give this account, which must be dishonest: "This bullet is worth more than your head. If you don't do what you're told; threatened his sister would be raped if the job was not done correctly," a threat which has a strange echo in another threat he refers to elsewhere but of an entirely different kind; told he had to take people to the back of the police station and murder them. The reason I can say that that account has to be a lie is because throughout his interviews with the investigators, he makes it absolutely plain there was no specific threat of any kind. He repeatedly says, "I knew I would be killed," but asked if there was any threat, denies it. There was none. He told Dr. Duits he had to kill with his head turned away. We know that's untrue. The photograph sequence, which barely needs to be shown, probably etched in our memories, the photograph sequence shows he had no difficulty facing the people he was killing, although in that case, of course, he was killing a man from behind. Van den Bussche was told that he was forced to kill by superiors and would have been killed, and he then raised this graphic account of going on his knees to beg not to be allowed to go on, something he'd never said or even hinted at before. Those accounts, the Chamber may conclude, don't really fit one with another; they don't fit with reality; they certainly don't fit with the descriptions given of his behaviour by all the witnesses. I come back to one of the very first things I said this morning, one of the things I raised with the psychiatrist, if you need someone to do dirty work for you, the easiest way of knowing whether the person is going to do it is to ask him. That's the way you get a volunteer. As the doctors were good enough to agree with me yesterday, this is the sort of man who would be a volunteer. Can I trouble you now with the second document, which looks far more alarming than it is because it's big, but we're going to deal with it quite swiftly, I hope. I have to review the evidence on the counts, and so this is a document of the nature which I've explained. It seeks, so far as possible, to deal by summary with the evidence in the case in a chronological order, and so it may be helpful for the Chamber generally, I hope it will be, although I expect the Chamber's own work on the case will include something similar maybe, but nevertheless it's a chronological document. The left-hand column is self-explanatory, events and dates, and we'll also see reference to particular count numbers. The witness testimony comes in the middle, and to the right, where it's been possible to connect what the defendant said of an event with the event, that's set out there with appropriate references. The document changes form very slightly when we move beyond material that can be put in any chronological order because it's impossible to date it, so that starts at page 68, the page numbers being in the bottom right-hand corner. It's impossible to know how long I would take were I to take you through all of the rather limited number of passages I've highlighted, but if I try for ten minutes and see how far I go, then I may be able to review the approach generally. One can use this document to tell the story and to remind ourselves of the evidence concerning this man in a pretty orderly way, and if the Chamber will forgive me simply using page references and either "the right-hand column" or "the middle column," I can probably proceed quite swiftly. Page 1. In the right-hand column, he sets out coming as brothers to Brcko, learning of the blowing of bridges, and being given lists. Page 2. We can see that on his own evidence, right-hand column, three lines down, his understanding was that as many Muslims as possible had to be killed and that Brcko should become a Serbian town. That account, of course, fits with the evidence of Witness K, central column, who saw the list on his desk and who, three lines up from the bottom of that passage, recognised prominent people as being named, well-known people. It fits with an answer given, foot of the page, central column, to Judge Riad. When Witness A, a year ago, was answering questions, he said: "Judging by what was happening ... Muslims ... needed to be killed and, if possible ... eradicated." Page 3. In his general defence, the defendant both acknowledged, right-hand column, middle of the page, that the people he killed were never given a chance to defend themselves and were completely helpless, but in his defence, two-thirds of the way down, said there was no one he could appeal to, and then when asked, "Did you protest or question the list you were given?" his answer was, "No, to be honest." Page 4, top of the page, right-hand column. I remind the Chamber that he was a party to the plan in the sense that he was informed. Just how low down the chain was he, this man who was informed in advance of what was planned? He told us, through his interview, that he was at a checkpoint in Srpska Varos on the railway when, on the 3rd or 4th of May, he was taken for a special task. We can turn over page 5 and go straight to page 6. I remind the Chamber that he spent some time at the barracks threatening Muslim detainees. Second entry down, middle column, Witness G told you that his threats to them were that 70 per cent of them should be killed, 30 per cent beaten up, and maybe three per cent were all right. "All of you are going to come to me," he said, "cursing their balija mothers." Only when that witness, Witness G, got to Luka was Jelisic recognised. The next entry from Witness N, at Laser, had him threatening to kill 80 Muslims, saying that he had killed 80 Muslims and threatening to kill all those before him. As to Laser, there's been some challenge, at some stage it being suggested, I think, he wasn't there introducing himself at Adolf, but at the bottom of this page, the right-hand column, the defendant himself acknowledged being at Laser, and he said there that the people were either in Laser or in number 13, and they all came from there to create the Luka camp. Over to page 7. The witnesses, in the middle column, for about this period include the witness, and it's right at the top of page 7, this is Witness L, reporting his saying, "My name is Goran Jelisic, Adolf the second. The first one was in Germany and I'm Adolf 2." That was when he took out a list and read some names. Further down the same page, in the middle, a claim overheard by Witness N that he'd killed 80 Muslims and would finish them all. Then the passage of cross-examination, which of course advances not on the imagination of Mr. Greaves but on instructions he's given by the defendant, who said, "It is not accepted that Goran Jelisic went to the Laser company and identified himself as Adolf and that in that regard, that witness has got the wrong person ..." As I say, if you look to the right-hand side of this page, top entry, three lines down, the defendant himself, in interview, said he was taken to Laser as he didn't know how to get there. He offered to discuss Laser later on, if one looks at the foot of the page, but maybe that didn't go any further by way of admissions from him. Page 8, please. We come effectively to the first count, although it's probably the last count in the list, Count 44. This man, so reluctant, as he would ask you to accept, to do what he was doing was reported by Witness N, the foundation of Count 44, to have said that the soldiers on his arrival at the Laser company were looking for members of the wealthy families whom he named. Other soldiers entered, and one identified himself as "Adolf from Bijeljina. He told us to put our valuables and documents on the table." Money, but not the documents, were picked up. We come then to the 6th of May, to what would appear to be an early or the earliest killing, the one that is evidenced by the sequence of photographs. The Chamber will recall not only the sequence of photographs, distressing as it is, but that that lane down which the defendant pursued his quarry already had at the end of it at least two bodies of men already killed. As to that, he said, this was a baptism of fire. Page 8, bottom entry, right-hand side. And he was told about the photographers being there to do it for him. Was it a baptism by fire? How had these other bodies come to be at the end of the same lane? May we go to page 10. I just look at the interpreters' booth to see that I'm not going too fast. Page 10. We come to Count 6 and 7, the killing of Hasan Jasarevic. The witness in the middle describes the killing. Perhaps Witness Q's account is more interesting at this stage for what the witness said the defendant did immediately after killing Hasan Jasarevic. "After that he came to the kiosk and hit me on the head and the neck with his baton, pointed his pistol at me, started asking me about the Green Berets and the ZNG's, and starting cursing my Muslim mother." At the foot of the page, Witness P gives his account, which we find on page 11. This victim -- who can blame him -- started to cry and to plead about his wife and children. That worked for nothing, and the Chamber will have in mind what the defendant now relies on in interviews and with psychiatrists by way of protestation that if anyone pleaded with him he would rather shoot himself. Staying on page 11. The man from Sinteraj, the young man, as the right-hand column on page 11, four lines down, reveals, handed to Jelisic at the police station, killed with two bullets. Page 12, Count 10. The unhappy man known as Papa, who had plainly taken a part in local politics before the war. The evidence in the middle column, the answers of Witness J: He "had a baton and was beating Papa, telling him to hurry, to move quicker, this was the last time he was seeing his town." The version -- the sanitised version of the defendant on the right-hand side, halfway down page 12: "I was handed Ahmet Hodzic in front of the duty booth," and followed the same script. Three lines on: "I can't remember that I beat him. I don't think I did because it was not ordered to me to beat him." Then over the page, when the account of the witness is put to him, on our page 13, five lines down: "If that person had started begging or asking, I would rather have killed myself." Three lines further on: "If he had spoken one word to me, I would have done something to save him." Page 14, please. Count 12, the murder of Suad. The evidence from Witness J. The Chamber will remember the strong man relied upon to carry the bodies and then to be the last person to be killed. So his fitness saves his life and brings him here. He was able to describe the killing of this unhappy man who cried -- middle of the page on page 14: "What happened when he cried? Goran said he didn't like men who cried and ordered him to start off. The man begged to be left alive because he had a small child at home. Goran did not heed that." On the right-hand side, asked about this, he accepted that he'd killed this man. About eight lines down on the right-hand side he said this of beating, denying the allegations of beating made about this killing: "If there were orders to beat someone, then it would be with a baton. I'm not much for beating people." At the foot of page 14, the waste of this live revealed in his own answers, page 30 of the interview: "I think Suad was younger, was a young person, but I couldn't come to any data on why he had been accused. My belief is that people who were held in cell 13 were either politically engaged ..." and then he goes on to deal with the families. Page 15. I remind the Chamber of how he cursed the Muslims he controlled as balijas; Witness J and Witness Q. Now, at the foot of this page, he ordered them to sing Serbian songs, beating those who failed. Over the page to page 16. Witness P, how the man made a mistake and would then be hit. The Chamber will be asking itself the question: How does this fit with what is advanced on his behalf as mitigating material? More of the same, at the foot of page 16, from Witness Q, with the defendant conducting the Muslims with a baton and also saying that they could just be run over by a truck. Page 17, the murders of Korenjic and Lucic, not in the indictment, and admitted to by the defendant, as I said, going to a limited degree beyond what was necessarily formally proved against him. At the foot of page 17, aware of that refrigerator truck or trucks. So powerful an image in, I suspect, all our minds, although the Chamber may think that though the photographs of Jelisic shooting the men in the alleyway may be a powerful and unforgettable image, even that may pale into insignificance beside the view of the open grave which showed the overall callous disregard for life of which these killings was an integral part. Page 18, coming to the end of what happened at the SUP office. The Chamber will remind itself, and I needn't take you into the detail, of the man who was both murdered and disfigured, castrated before being thrown on the lorry. So at page 19 we come to Luka camp. Page 20. He advanced in interview that the reason he was given the name "Adolf" was for the Motorola. That is an assertion not supported elsewhere and the Chamber may doubt its reliability. In the middle of page 20. Witness A, a year ago, told us that this defendant claimed to have killed 150 people. Page 21. The same witness saying, at the end of the passage transcribed, that only 5 to 10 of them there would be lucky enough to leave alive. Witness D speaking of the same point in time, the beginning of Luka, saying that as many balijas as possible should be killed, attributing that to the defendant. At page 22 there's more evidence summarised, including, in the evidence of Witness K, first the offensive remark that Muslims were reproducing to a great extent and that there was a lot of work to do to cleanse them. And in the second passage, in the middle of the page, where he explained how the defendant was the main figure in the camp, that everybody had to respect him, that he issued orders and wielded out fates. The witness told us that he repeated that he was the Serbian Adolf, copying the Nazi method of cleansing people. A different offensive description reported by Witness M, at the foot of that page: "Cleansing the Serbs of the extremist Muslims and balijas like one cleans the head of lice." This imagination -- it may be childish in some ways -- is it the imagination of someone just acting under orders or does it show completely full, individual responsibility? Page 23, Count 14. Two men, one, as we see in the evidence of Witness G, in the middle of the page, dealt with as a person who cursed a Serb woman's mother, taken out. And if we go over the page to page 24, we can see in the evidence of the witness, in the middle of the page, how they decided, callously decided, which one was to be killed by whom, and how, on the right-hand side of the page, how the defendant, in dealing with this matter, explained that Jasminko Cumurovic was finished with by the inspectors, told he was dangerous, so he took him to the corner of the hangar and killed him. He said, "Even after this murder, I could not find out. Nobody wanted to tell me why this man was guilty." The evidence of this killing, of course, continued with the evidence from Witness M, who gave that graphic account -- was it just made up or was it entirely true? -- of the defendant forcing the man who was killed first to lick the defendant's hand, and then shooting him. I can move now, I think, more quickly, having reminded the Chamber of much of the evidence. Page 26, the testimony of Danijel Ibrahamovic. Page 27, the killings of Huso and Smajl Zahirovic, the two brothers from Zvornik. At page 28 there's no evidence about that. He accepting the killing of only one of them, of course. We can go to page 30, just to remind ourselves of the reality of these acts. At the top of the page, Witness N, dealing with these brothers, giving Your Honours a graphic account of the beatings, the moanings, and the screams that were associated with such killings. Staying on page 30, the killing of up to five unknown men witnessed by Witness F, seeing a succession of people being taken around the corner of those buildings and shot. This all on the 8th of May. At the foot of the 8th of May, this unwilling executioner, as he would have you think he was, seen by Witness L counting money. And to remind you, at page 31, the defendant said this: "He showed me an amount of money and said that a man had given him money so that he would not kill him." The defendant said: "I took the money and I killed him nevertheless." Staying on page 31, early evidence from Witness B taken, I think, by Mr. Tochilovsky, it may have been Mr. Bowers, a year ago, and even with the diet of disturbing material that this Chamber, with its various compositions, must receive, evidence that may well have stayed with it, the three or four men called out time after time, one being selected by the defendant, his head placed on the grate, two others being obliged to carry him around the corner to the pile of bodies, reforming themselves as the remaining three people in front of the hangar from whom another would be chosen, dispatched, and carried, leaving two and sometimes one. The Witness B, who survived was it two or even three rounds of that particular form of roulette, perhaps being a most memorable witness for this Chamber. Over then now, please, to page 34, still on the 8th of May. According to Witness K, the defendant, in the lines of detainees, forcing them to sing Serbian songs. We turn on page 35 to the 9th of May, Counts 18 and 19, the beating and killing of Naza Bukvic. A woman, as Witness G told us, in the middle of the page, sitting on the grass, being beaten by Jelisic, complaining that her brother was a sniper. His account of this, on the right-hand side: "Did he have any conversation," foot of the page, "before he killed her?" He couldn't possibly. "I don't admit to it. I may have sworn at her. I may have cursed her," he says at the top of page 36. "I don't remember." That woman's father is the subject of the following counts, 20 and 21. The callous behaviour witnessed by Witness D, in the middle of the page, asked about the killing of this man, the witness explained that the unhappy Ahmetovic asked where his daughter was. Goran said: "You'll find out shortly." His explanation, he simply, on the right-hand side, he simply did the same to Naza. They were extreme nationalists. Page 37. The graphic and dreadful killing of the man carrying his own ear. Jelisic taunting the Muslims with the offer that they should kill him, the man begging to be killed, but Jelisic eventually doing it himself. It's worth noting, at page 37, on the right-hand side, last entry: "Personally I never fired at a dead body. There was no need for that." The Chamber will recall the last photographs in the sequence of photographs and ask itself questions about the accuracy of that statement. An unknown man is revealed as killed, at page 39, in the evidence of Witness D. This on the 9th of May. Accompanied, as we see, in the middle of the page, at the end of Witness D's transcript. "Did Goran say anything to the prisoner before he shot him? He did. What did he say? 'No reason why to waste time with you.'" The same death reflected further, at page 40, towards the evidence of Witness O, which is summarised in the middle of page 40, with Jelisic requiring that the man be held further to the ground so he couldn't move while he shot him. I turn over to page 42. To some degree, Your Honours, we have relied to very limited degree in this document on Annex 1, which was the material that accompanied the original guilty plea, and that explains the annotation for the 10th to the 12th of May, the beatings of those two people which, of course, was never the subject of evidence in this court. He accepts beating these two men. Further down the same page, 42, the man in his 70s killed by this defendant, too old, as the witnesses told you, to be a sniper. And, on the right-hand side, conceded by Jelisic as too old to have been a soldier, he saying he thought he was a political activist, despite his age. At page 43, you get some flavour of the nature of the beating. About six lines down, a short metal shovel with a wooden handle was spoken of by Witness H. The beating was, of course, eventually followed by the death. On page 44, Counts 36 and 37, the beating of Mohamed Bukvic. The defendant's explanation, right-hand corner of page 44: "The order was to beat him up. Because it was known that his brother-in-law" -- I beg your pardon: "His brother, son-in-law would come to fetch him." Then in the middle of page 44, "I don't deny he was beaten." Page 47, the Chamber will want to be reminded, again about a graphic piece of evidence, of the woman in the red sweater. As to her, the evidence given by Witness E, was that she arrived at the camp in a red van, shouting and crying she was not guilty and had doing nothing. The defendant arrived shortly after in another vehicle. He had with him, the witness thought, a sawn-off rifle that we've seen, the weapon he typically used. And two-thirds down this page: "He walked in her direction", the Chamber will remember, I think, she was seated in the area, "Got her by the scruff of the neck, drew her to one of the officers, made her fall, pushed her so she fell against the kerb, and fired at the back of her head, thus dispatching her from life," and that's repeated in the evidence over the page as well, but I needn't go into it. On page 48, there's the killing of a male nurse. On page 49, for about the 14th of May, some evidence of other killings are set out there and the beating of the Witness E himself. You can see in the central column of page 49 how somebody asked the defendant, "Shall this one beat him or the one in the black T-shirt?" The defendant gave instructions who should do the beating and, as we see further down the page, kicked him and beat him, despite protestations that the poor man, as he was judged to be, should be left. At page 50, I remind the Chamber that although, in a passage of his interview connected with Witness R, the defendant maintains he only ever signed and had access to one pass, that Witness E told you about and, I think, produced to you a pass signed "Adolf" that guaranteed his safe conduct. Indeed, as we can see at the foot of the entry for Witness E on page 50, Jelisic said that that pass meant that nobody would lay a finger on him, but he maintained, as I've already said, that he only ever issued one pass. What does his ability to issue passes in this camp or from this camp show of his authority? Page 51. We turn, on the 14th of May, to the arrival of the army major who stopped the killing, despite Jelisic's disquiet about that, and at the foot of 51, at about this same time, we come to Witness R himself. Just a few facts to remind you about for him. So 15.600 Deutschemarks, some of which belonged to the religious community, were taken; the defendant doesn't accept that but the Chamber has seen how he was able to move about, buy things, and live without apparent work, apart from maybe being in the army thereafter. The Chamber will remember the details of the killing of three detainees. There's a difference between Witness R and Witness S. Is it because one or other or both of them have come here to lie to you, or is it because, as was raised as a possibility yesterday in this Chamber, circumstances so terrifying may lead to differences in detail of account but the substance will remain the same? If the substance is correct, this man, by way of show and display, killed three men to show off to that man of strong character whom he did not kill by the game of Russian roulette. Can there be any doubt that that was one, at any event, of his underlying motives in producing men and having them beaten and killed in the way he did? As to the Russian roulette itself, did he click the trigger, as Witness S says? Did he not, as Witness R says, but rather say, "The Serbs need me" and take the gun away? Who would be likely to have the most accurate and vivid account? Who would be likely, in the circumstances in that terrifying room, to get it wrong, inaccurate? In any event, from everything that you have heard of this defendant, do you believe he would have the courage to take the risk of Russian roulette? A coward before the war, has there been anything shown to you to show you a man brave afterwards? He provided, of course, the pass for those people, and their ability to pass the checkpoints is something for the Chamber to consider. Does it fit with a man doing the menial but dreadful task of killing to the orders of others, or does his freedom of manoeuvre speak of something else? We can turn on to page 55. There's the killing of Adnan Kucalovic, Counts 38 and 39, dealt with in summary by Jelisic, at page 56, the right-hand side: "I went into the hangar to get him to ask, 'Is your brother in the Muslim army?' He didn't want to answer anything. I took him out of the hangar and killed him." Smail Ribic, not on the indictment; Witness B, the first person to be killed. We're now out of the strictly chronological order of the indictment but slotting things in that have uncertain dates. Then we come to page 57. Now, from page 57 -- no, I beg your pardon. Yes, page 57. We're still dealing with other killings, and I hope to move much more quickly. Witness B, I've already dealt with, the three or four volunteers at a time taken out of the hangar. Page 59. Further evidence that the Chamber will remind itself of from Witness A. The only other matter I can think of before the luncheon adjournment -- and I'm sorry not to have concluded, but perhaps I can make one other point about the evidence, see if there's anything else from this document that I need to review and then conclude my arguments by returning to the first document this afternoon, with your leave -- the only other piece of evidence that it might be helpful to remind you of at this stage is the evidence of the woman who came before you. You will remember, of course, that her evidence was associated with the disappearance from the courtroom of the defendant after she'd given the first passage of her evidence and her desire to speak in his presence and not to give evidence in his absence. She spoke of her own dreadful treatment at the hands of men other than Jelisic, and she also spoke, as you will recall, of recurring beatings and killings of men produced, as it were, to her or in front of her, although she and the others had to look down, beatings that were apparently followed by death; evidence that fits, you see, with evidence that you've had from elsewhere, for example, from the imam; evidence that shows the Chamber may judge objectives oblique to the mere performance of someone else's orders and that speak volumes for the authority and independent acts of this man. I'm sorry not to have finished. We started a little later than we expected, and I will try and reduce what remains so that Mr. Greaves can have the majority of the afternoon.

utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, first of all, Mr. Nice. It's 1.00, and we will resume at 2.30. Court stands adjourned. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can resume the hearing now. Please have the accused brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nice, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. I have only a few further references to the second document I presented. I'm starting at page 60, in some limited degree backtracking just to remind Your Honours about the evidence of Witness A, who dealt with the people being called out to be killed, who reminded you in his evidence about how people had to go out in the mornings to clear the blood from the grates, and who estimated, and this can be seen at the foot of page 60, about five lines up, that if he multiplied 25 to 30 by the groups of 4, dealing with the number of times people were taken out, why it was his calculation that some 150 people must have been taken out and not returned to the hangar. Then over the page at 61, still in his evidence, we see part of one of his accounts of a killing, which is graphic, where the defendant was forcing people onto the asphalt, to keep their heads on that drainage grate so that he could kill them with less inconvenience in the form of split blood. The same witness, in the middle of page 61, dealt with a particularly unpleasant incident where this man was speaking of a Muslim who was married to a Serbian woman, and I needn't necessarily defile the air with the precise way he expressed his opinion on that occasion, but it's there. Towards the foot of page 61, and I think this is very nearly the last page I deal with in detail, a few minor references hereafter, is an image that the Chamber may or may not have found particularly hard to dispel, not least because of the civilisation that is afforded to the defendant both here in court when he is granted water whenever he wants it, and as we heard from the psychiatric examiner, interestingly granted refreshment again, specifically whenever he wanted it, said to be demanding in respect of that. The Chamber will recall the file of men crossing the alley to get their water in fear. I think they went by threes, did they not? And one man dropped his bottle of water because it was wet, no doubt out of fear. That alone sealed his fate, and he was called to the grate by Jelisic and killed. Now, unless that evidence is entirely false, the figment of the witness's imagination, it is evidence that is completely at odds with any and every assertion by this man that he was simply acting according to orders. So we can move to page 63, centre of the page, the period after the 18th of May, 18th, 19th of May, when the camp had fallen under the command of Monika's brother, his young girlfriend's brother. According to the witness Didic, he still attended, did Jelisic, and came back and looked around, and indeed in his interviews, I'm afraid I don't have the page immediately at hand, he in his interviews acknowledged that after the killings he went back to look at the prisoners. You will recall evidence of one of the witnesses saying how he broke in, frustrated, you may think, at the interdiction against further killings and expressed his desire to kill again. We see at the foot of 63 the beginning of the account of the beating of Amir Didic, Counts 40 and 41. Because of the comparatively lesser offence that it is I'll take less time with it, but, nevertheless, you will notice at page 64 the sanitised version emerging, the witness speaking of the degree of the assault, Coca-Cola bottles broken against his head, beaten until he fainted, with, on the right-hand side, the defendant acknowledging no more than hitting with a baton, never using any of the other weapons spoken of by the witness. Page 67, if the Court would be so good. The chart simply deals with the evidence of the mass graves, which, in a sense, is not so relevant, save to say that you can see, and this is a passage I referred to earlier, that in his interview on the 23rd of July, Jelisic was being kept informed at the end of 1992 or 1993, as he would say, with what was known not about the original depositing of the bodies but of the removal of the bodies. The Chamber may recall the evidence of the exhumations, that there was the clearest possible evidence of graves being robbed, no doubt with the purpose of obscuring from investigators of this institution where they might otherwise be found. So he seemed to be being kept informed. At page 69 and following, we have a compilation of extracts from the transcript that may go to demonstrate de facto authority or control in Luka. I've touched on many of them already. I'll just draw your attention to a couple more. On page 69 itself, a third of the way down, Witness B describing the defendant as not only being boastful and arrogant, but line 2, expressly saying he was the boss there. Over at page 70, at the foot of the page, Witness I, in answer to a question from our Presiding

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TO THE EFFECT
utterances.text: "Was the impression of directing operations or of having things carried out on the orders of others," the witness gave this answer: "I could say that he was both. He carried out orders but also selected his victims through his own free will. He could have not shot someone even if he were told to do so, but he did quite a few things on his own." At page 71, at the top, Witness A's account of Jelisic saying he was the director of the collection centre, determining who would be brought there and interrogated, who would be killed, who would be released, words to the effect that there was not a single balija who was not guilty, in the defendant's belief. And then the second extract from the same witness dealing, "... after one balija less," with the witness's observation: "I don't think this was killing on orders. I think this was killing out of pleasure, out of some kind of hate against my people." Towards the foot of the page, the graphic evidence from E, hard almost to accept unless one abandons civilisation and recognises what was going on there. And is there any reason that he would make this up? He said that a man came in -- another man came in and said to Adolf that a victim's ears, and nose, and eyes had been cut or gouged. Adolf's reply was to go and kill the man who on that account was still living. At page 73, there's a collection of the passages where Jelisic has dealt with the number of Muslims he claims to have killed, and one can see the figures, casting one's eyes down the page, "80," "53," "54." At the bottom of the page, saying once, "... I've killed seven people so far ... another eight, and that will do for the day." Over the page at our page 74 and in the middle of the page. There is reference to the percentages who would survive and his expectation that once they had survived, they'd see him in town and buy him a drink. Further references to number, the number 68, in particular, from Witness F. At the foot of the page, this graphic account: "... as the Serb Adolf turned over his automatic gun ... to a person ... going by the name..." the name is given, saying, "There. Now is your chance to make a notch on the butt, because after you kill your balijas, your Muslim persons, then you should know the number..." and he went off to have a drink and this other man would relieve him. On that same page, page 75, just over halfway down, from Witness L: "Yes. He said to me that in the morning, when he would get up, before he would take his coffee, he'd have to kill 20 to 30 people." At page 76, under a collection of transcript passages dealing with anti-Muslim behaviour, a man who claims he was acting only under orders, from Witness F, picking up a man on his knees, saying, "I must be crazy. I'm helping a balija to stand up and I've got my hands soiled." There are various other passages quoted there to remind the Chamber if it finds them helpful. At page 81, dealing with the proposition that he was not the person with authority, Witness R, at the foot of the page, told you -- this is for the 15th of May or thereabouts -- that he had a folder, a plasticised folder. He opened it and with a pencil made circles around names, and then went through that page quickly, circling other numbers. Was he really a man without the ability to exercise his own initiative, this man who, at any time, could travel freely around Brcko, past the checkpoints? Then finally for this document, page 82. In the enjoyment, if that is the word, of killings and his inability to be tired of what he was doing, from Witness B, this description: "... I think that he took pleasure in doing this because he was so powerful, he was viewed as a god. It was nothing for him to kill a man. He believed himself to be the most powerful person in the world, and he was, in Brcko. I cannot understand this. He was a young man, a handsome man, and to do this ..." Witness F describes how, following a killing, or just before one, I can't remember which, he and the other guards would meet and laugh heartily, and the same witness, towards the end of the page, another man speaking to him offered to take over and to give the defendant a rest, the defendant replying that this was a job which he didn't find difficult. When he felt like having a drink, he would count on that other man's offer of help. Can I respectfully invite the Chamber to return to the other document which we left at page 21 and which I will be able to conclude, by further cuts, quite swiftly. We were at paragraph 49. We've passed that schedule of evidence. Discriminatory behaviour is, of course, a constituent element to some offences, and the degree of discriminatory element may be an aggravating factor. I don't need to read the rest of that paragraph; I've summarised all the material in dealing with the evidence. At the foot of page 22, I deal very shortly with the limited evidence there is of what happened afterwards. At page 23, we hear from Dr. Duits about his leaving the camp, allegedly confessing to the Muslim lawyer, from whom we've heard nothing, of his going home; of his wanting to inform an international organisation, if any of this is true, and unless that relates to our Witness Q; of shooting himself in the foot. You've already heard this morning how the dates in September 1992 are rather later than one might have thought. He was already in the army. One document shows the left side, another the right. The report from the doctors, of course, says nothing about this being any self-inflicted act. I repeat, paragraph 52 of this document, that the Defence evidence generally is capable of the interpretation that the defendant may, to a degree, have been setting up witnesses. If so, that aggravates the position for him. Gravity of the offence. The Trial Chamber, in our respectful submission, must consider the gravity, and the Tadic Trial Chamber observed at sentencing that the specific harm caused to victims and their families by the defendant is of paramount importance. There are numerous, if not innumerable, victims of this man's crimes. In the Tadic case itself, the degree of victimisation is significantly less than in this case, it may be the Chamber will conclude, and the involvement directly in killings are on an entirely different and lesser scale. Comparisons of suffering may be difficult, but the Chamber will, no doubt, have consistency with other sentences in mind when it sentences this man, and in evaluating the gravity of the offence, the Trial Chamber must consider the suffering, physical and psychological, of all victims. May we respectfully say, not, as it were, specifically to this Chamber, but as a problem facing sentencing judges around the world, and particularly here, that there is a danger that time spent analysing the psychological state of the defendant reduces the focus of attention that should be on the dead and on surviving victims, whose suffering either cannot be, because they're dead, or has not been, because there is never the time, tested, save to a very limited degree, yet it is those victims, dead and surviving, whose interests should come first. The defendant has committed several acts constituting crimes against humanity judged by the Chamber recently as a more serious offence than an ordinary war crime and should ordinarily entail a heavier penalty. I'm alive, I think, to the existence of the minority decision of Judge Robinson on that topic. Paragraph 55. The defendant committed crimes with particular cruelty in a merciless manner, we've gone over all that, but in this paragraph, it may be worth proposing that he is clearly revealed as intending to cripple their psyches and destroy their personalities. I omitted to mention this morning, but the Chamber may recall, that the woman we referred to, the woman whose evidence the defendant nearly avoided or missed, spoke not only of seeing the men beaten and then taken out and killed, but she spoke of how Jelisic said, "Those who are left will be there only for menial jobs. You," and she was a professional woman, no longer able to work as a result of all this, no longer able to pursue her caring profession, "You," he said, "will never work in that occupation again." We can only hope that he was wrong because, of course, it is possible that the cathartic exercise of coming here will have helped her in her recovery, but until today's date, for different reasons, he's turned out to be right. Nothing was done to protect these detainees who were at the mercy of the defendant and much to abuse them. Paragraph 56. I think I'm following the criteria set out in Tadic to a degree. The murders and beatings of the detainees in Luka was part of a wider pattern of extermination, as Mr. Ralston told us, and when survivors were released, they couldn't stay in Brcko, they had become refugees with no residence or property and a small chance of employment, many being transformed from independent, self-sufficient citizens to those dependent on the largess of others.
