Almost none have returned to Brcko, and although, of course, this defendant is not in any way responsible for everything that those victims lost, as the Tadic Chamber has found, the general environment may be considered as relevant to the increased infliction of pain. Personal history. We are encouraged, I think, to deal with this. We have dealt with it substantially already. In paragraph 57, acknowledging as a possibility that youth and personality problems might, in other circumstances, be considered in fashioning an appropriate sentence, the Prosecution's position is that these long-standing problems, first of all, do not permit the Chamber to say that he is not a continuing danger to society and would respectfully invite the Chamber to be aware of hypothetical questions about his behaviour in future circumstances, whether in war or peace. That is hardly to the point. By his personality, he is capable of being a danger, and it is not possible to say he is not. In any event, for the purposes of retribution for him and deterrence for him and others, the crimes are of such gravity as to deny the man benefit from his personality. Role of offence, under paragraph 58, is another factor to be considered. I think we've probably covered that fully already. Page 26, paragraph 59. Policy considerations in favour of strict punishment. Paragraph 60. The deterrence function of the International Tribunal should be the main guiding policy principle for sentencing determination. In the recent Tadic sentencing judgement, the Trial Chamber said: "The unique mandate of the International Tribunal of putting an end to the widespread violations of international humanitarian law warrants particular consideration in respect of the purpose of sentencing." Citing the Celebici case and making reference to ICTY and ICTR case law, the Chamber emphasised that "... deterrence is probably the most important factor in the assessment of appropriate sentences for violations of international humanitarian law." The Erdemovic sentencing judgement highlights the overriding importance at stigmatising the most serious violations of international humanitarian law through sentencing. Further, the Chamber can consider the general practice for prison sentences in the courts of the former Yugoslavia as guidance but not as anything that is in any way binding. Capital punishment existed at the time, although it has been abolished by constitutional amendment in certain Yugoslavia republics other than Bosnia and Herzegovina. It is argued, I think, in Tadic, that the most directly applicable statutory provisions of the former Yugoslavia are those under crimes against peace and international law, which deal with a number of criminal acts, including killings, tortures, inhumane treatments, and so on. Providing that they shall be punished by no less than five years strict imprisonment or by the death penalty. The code that sets out that offence or that punishment sets out factors to be taken into account, to be found at the top of page 28, legal limits for the punishment of the offence; purpose of punishment; circumstances which influence severity; degree of criminal responsibility; motives; intensity of threat or injury to the protected object; circumstances of the commission of the offence; perpetrator's past life; perpetrator's personal circumstances and his behaviour after the commission of the offence, a catalogue for which, in our respectful submission, the defendant is incapable of finding material to fill any element of that catalogue, significantly or at all. The Tadic sentencing judgement referred to the importance of reconciliation, saying the unique mandate of the International Tribunal, contributing to the restoration and maintenance of peace in the former Yugoslavia warrants particular consideration in respect of the purpose of sentencing, a significant factor in the case against a defendant who is known widely and perhaps throughout Bosnia and Herzegovina as a mass killer, who referred to himself as the Serbian Adolf. Paragraph 66 sets out what is perhaps obvious and already stated about the purposes of these proceedings. I turn to paragraph 67 on page 29. The defendant seeks an advantage from his position, as he asserts, low in the chain of responsibility. We invite the Chamber to have in mind that in any war, military and political leaders need willing executioners to do their criminal acts for them. They keep their hands, the leaders that is, keep their hands clean. Without enthusiastic executioners like this defendant, the crimes would never occur. The aims of the criminal leadership could and would be thwarted. This Trial Chamber has a unique opportunity to send a strong message to all perpetrators, at whatever level in a chain of command, that commission of crimes like these brings vulnerability, for all who are involved, to the full weight of international justice. In the event, contrary to the thrust of our submission, that the Chamber accepts that the defendant performed any good acts after the killings in Brcko, it may be prudent to recall the wisdom of the Nuremberg jurisprudence, which explained how it is not an unusual phenomenon in life to find an isolated good deed emerging from an evil man. Because of convenience, caprice, or even a sudden ephemeral gleam of benevolence forcing its way through a calloused heart, even a murderer can help a child to safety. A grim humour can cause a slayer to save his intended victim. But whatever the cause which motivated "X's benevolence to Y," the quotation continues, the kind deed is not enough to obliterate his indifference to the wholesale suffering of which he could not but be aware, and to alleviate which, in spite of his protestations, he did little or nothing. There is no evidence suggesting that the defendant displayed benevolence at Luka camp. Even if he had done so, it could not have obliterated the extreme gravity of his criminal acts for which he has been convicted. The sentence on the defendant, in our submission, should reflect the magnitude of the horrifying crimes that occurred and the suffering that was caused by him. He cries out effectively for mercy. He showed none. World opinion, it might be safe to conclude, would not want him to be shown any, and it is our submission that this Chamber should show him none and should impose on him the maximum sentence of life imprisonment. Unless I can assist the Chamber further, that concludes our submissions.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We do not have the Judge's microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We thank you. It's 20 after 3.00. Without any further ado, we will give the floor to Mr. Greaves for the Defence of Goran Jelisic. Please proceed, Mr. Greaves.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: In opening, what I have to say to Your Honours this afternoon, I firstly wish to make three points. I firstly wish to take up my learned friend Mr. Nice's observations the privilege of practising in this Court. I have been fortunate enough to be involved in two substantial and significant trials before this Tribunal. I hope, although others may disagree, that I have made a modest contribution to its jurisprudence in one or the other trial. I was brought up to believe that the task of Defence counsel, indeed his role that he had to play in the criminal process, had one aspect which was particularly important, and that is that he must at all times stand up as a bulwark against the overwhelming power of a potentially oppressive state, and with all the facilities and faculties at his disposal, fearlessly yet properly to advocate the cause of his client. In opening his address to Your Honours, my learned friend was helpful enough and kind enough to draw to Your Honours' attention the numerous members of the Prosecution team. I ask Your Honours to remember this: This is a trial of a single defendant, not a multiple-defendant trial. The point I have to make is this: He identified to Your Honours the extensive and substantial team that he has available to him: Leading counsel; co-counsel; assisted when required, at the drop of a hat by Mr. Bergsmo; a legal officer; a case manager; two investigators; and another person who, whilst counsel are doubtlessly occupied in court, is beavering away in the background producing documents; and then finally, some interns working free, adding their shoulders to the wheel; and he perhaps forgot to mention interpreters, who are employed by the Office of the Prosecutor as and when required, none of these restricted in any way as to the amount of time that they can spend on the preparation of the case. Well, I'm going to draw to Your Honours' attention and commend, where it is appropriate, those members of the Defence in the way that my learned friend so kindly commended his colleagues. Leading counsel Mr. Londrovic; myself; legal assistant Mr. Babic; one investigator; an interpreter, the long suffering Ms. Zivkovic, who has had to put up with my poor temper and tantrums from time to time. That's it. The legal assistant who has not been permitted to come to The Hague upon payment by the Tribunal. If we wanted him to come here and have his services here at the trial we were going to have to pay for it. The total hours that he was permitted to work restricted to 250. My interpreter, a constant battle to get hours permitted for her to work for me, and a struggle even to have her allowed to enable me to communicate with my client during the course of the trial. During non-trial periods counsel is restricted to 23 hours' work of paid work a week, and as we speak, there are plans afoot to restrict yet further the paid work and paid working conditions of the Defence. It is for others who listen to what I say to judge whether that even begins to look like genuine equality of arms. I have my own view of that particular aspect. The second matter is this -- and it concerns an extremely important issue in this case -- it goes to the issue of the medical reports: The Defence, and I am grateful to my learned friend in what appears to be an apparent concession that this is so, have plainly been put at a serious disadvantage as regards the presentation of medical evidence in this case. The Prosecution have been allowed to utilise the services of a psychiatrist who was placed under no restrictions either by the Registry or by the doctor herself as to whether that witness could quote and rely upon her examinations, diagnoses, and treatment in coming to the conclusions which he did in his report, and it is a matter of note that the Prosecution relied specifically upon some of the doctor's statements. I refer Your Honour to the transcript in today's hearing at pages 26 and 27; 26, line 21 to 27, 9. In our submission, these circumstances render it unfair that the Prosecution should be allowed to rely upon that report and upon the evidence of Dr. Duits, procured as it was under the circumstances considerably more advantageous than those afforded to the Defence. To do otherwise, we submit, would be a clear and unambiguous breach of the fair trial provisions that are guaranteed to the defendant under Articles 20 and 21. And I remind Your Honours that you have significant powers not just to evaluate evidence but to exclude evidence if so doing is required by the need to ensure a fair trial, outweighing any probative value that evidence may have. The third matter is this: Shortly before Your Honours came into court this morning, the Prosecution produced to the Defence what amounts to 130 pages of documentation, which has also been placed before Your Honours. There was, as I understood it, an order in this case that there should be no written briefs, and that was a matter that was discussed at the Status Conference. We were told yesterday that a skeleton argument would be produced for Your Honours. We note the document has been produced. We note that the size and the fact of its presentation has elicited no comment from Your Honours. Beyond that, we do not comment upon it. I turn now to the matters that involve the defendant directly. Seven and a half years after the events which erupted in north-eastern Bosnia, Goran Jelisic must now face the consequences of what he did and pay an inevitable price for what took place in Brcko in May 1992. We wish to make it plain that anything we say today is intended in no way to diminish the gravity of the taking of human life; in no way to diminish the gravity of ill-treating one's fellow human beings; in no way to diminish the gravity of the consequences for the families and friends of those who are left behind. Goran Jelisic has, today and on the date which Your Honours sentence him, to face up to that, and he knows it and accepts it. It must, however, be said that despite what the Prosecution has said about this matter, that until the 8th of November of this year, Your Honours and the public had only heard one side of the character and life of Goran Jelisic. One of the tasks I have set myself today is to present to Your Honours another more balanced side of this young man. We must cast our minds back to May 1992. We have heard in this case a considerable degree of evidence about the kind of person that Goran Jelisic was until war broke out in his country. In 1992, Goran Jelisic was still a young man, then aged 23. We respectfully submit that his age is one matter that you should properly and carefully consider. By all accounts, whatever the problems of his homelife may have been, he comes from a decent and respectable family, and no one who had met the parents and sister of the defendant could gainsay that proposition in any way. Until war erupted in the spring and summer of 1992, Goran Jelisic was someone who had lived an essentially ordinary life, albeit interspersed with moments of criminality. During the past three weeks, we have heard a considerable body of evidence that before the war he lived the kind of life that countless young men across Europe live today. He liked girls. By our lights, he makes inappropriate comments about them, though no one is prepared to make any sort of convention to him coming from a different culture where such remarks may still be thought acceptable. The Prosecution would have you believe that that is a damning and unredeeming feature of this defendant, but sadly, the Prosecution is wilfully blind to any sense of normality in this young man. He liked to hang around the bars of Bijeljina with his circle of friends. He liked to drink. He liked to smoke and he liked to party with his friends. He was a passionate fisherman. He was employed, by and large. Not a good job, but there's no sign that he was anything other than a perfectly normal man in his early 20s. I say that; of course, he got in trouble with the police, but that's not unusual in this modern age of ours. It may well have come as a surprise to Your Honour to learn the extent to which he was a friend of and fraternised with the Muslim community. The stereotypical view that one can have of the events that took place in Bosnia and Herzegovina in the early and mid '90s is one of unrestrained and deep-seated ethnic dislike. Of course, that's not true. Before these things happened, people were quite content to mix across ethnic lines and indeed that is very much the history of Bosnia itself. Those who are keen on Bosnia as an idea will emphasise to you that that was an important feature of its culture, and I can recall being lectured firmly about that by Edina Residovic, who appeared in the Celebici case, who is a staunch supporter of her country and of the fact that it is a multi-racial or was a multi-racial and multi-ethnic society. We submit that prior to the war, this defendant was, in fact, someone who had exhibited absolutely no sign whatever of ethnic hatred, ethnic dislike at all. It goes beyond that. He actively sought out the friendship of Muslims, and there is abundant evidence, you may think, that the vast majority of his friends were, in fact, Muslim. There is, you may think, no evidence whatever to contradict that proposition. The Prosecution dismisses, that saying, "Well, everybody was friendly in any event, and, therefore, it doesn't count." They've, remember, missed the point, we submit, because the point is this: The evidence in the case is he was friendly to Muslims before the war; he was friendly to Muslims during the war; he was friendly to Muslims after the war. So there is a degree of consistency. Of course, they have to attack the first part to demonstrate that during the war and after the war his acts of kindness to the Muslims were simply self-serving acts designed to set up somehow a defence or mitigation for the offences which he had committed. The fact of the matter is his friendship with Muslims is a consistent one and one which stretches back throughout his adult life. That, we submit, is an extremely important feature of this case. There is no evidence in the case, we submit, that prior to the war this defendant ever showed a single racist attitude, said anything with a racist connotation, did anything to anybody which had a racist connotation to it. You may think that he was, in fact, entirely lacking in such thoughts. It is at that point that the Prosecution have a difficulty because they have not even begun to try and explain how it is that suddenly, for a period of perhaps only 18 days, in May 1992, Goran Jelisic suddenly changed and became a blood-thirsty killer, glorying in his trade, and then suddenly, when he ceases to be occupied in that business, he reverts to having his Muslim friends whom he helps, in some cases, by ferrying them across the river at considerable personal risk to himself. They have not explained that. They have not demonstrated any reason why that should be so. There is no evidence in this case whatever that before the war Goran Jelisic took part in politics, in particular, in the brand of politics which could be described as hardened and ultranationalist, that has given rise to so much of the nasty brutishness, which those of us who have been involved in these cases have heard far too often. Of course, when considering Goran Jelisic as a person, it's right to say that there did come a time when he went off the rails. There is nothing unusual in that. Those of us, like my learned friend for the Prosecution, who have practised for many years as advocates in the criminal courts, both as prosecutors and defenders, we have come across hundreds of defendants like Goran Jelisic who have gone from hitherto blameless existence and blameless lives into a cycle of substance abuse and criminal activity designed to support that habit. In that sense, Goran Jelisic is not unlike many other young men across Europe. It's all too familiar a picture. The fact is there did come a time when he engaged in serious criminal activity and he started to deal dishonestly in cheques. He was caught, prosecuted, and sentenced for those crimes. An interesting feature of this, and something for which both he and his witnesses are castigated, is that he concealed it from his friends, and some effort has been made by the Prosecution to belittle the judgement of those friends and to challenge the closeness of such friendships because they were unaware that their friend had slipped into that activity. We submit that that is an unrealistic and unfair approach to take. In the real world, there are many who conceal activities of that kind, and who in this room has never heard of a case where it's suddenly revealed that some person, otherwise thought to be upright and decent and law-abiding, is in fact discovered to be in serious trouble with the law, to the utter astonishment of family, friends, and community? In this case, we submit that friends of Goran Jelisic were essentially decent people. It comes as no surprise, perhaps, that Goran Jelisic sought to hide from them, those decent people, that he was in fact living a life of crime. That, prior to May 1992, was indeed the dark side of Goran Jelisic. Then came the events of spring and summer of 1992. Yugoslavia, a strong and cohesive and unified entity for a long time, suddenly sprang apart, and suddenly the people of towns like Brcko found themselves having to choose one side or the other. People who had been friends or neighbours for years found themselves on nominally opposing sides in a thoroughly nasty and brutish civil war. No one would deny for a moment that Goran Jelisic played a role, and a serious role, in the nastiness and brutishness which that conflict threw up. The Prosecution paints a picture of Goran Jelisic at that time in but one colour. They say that for a short period, he was an enthusiastic, willing, and glorying killer, killing Muslims, although it's not entirely explained why he should suddenly have become that. They say he has no redeeming qualities at all. They accuse him of lacking remorse and of profiting from the situation of Muslims. It's been their position all along, and, no doubt, they felt that, with the evidence they were proposing to present, they were onto a sure thing. We respectfully submit that, unfortunately for that proposition, evidence has in fact been presented to this Tribunal which undermines the Prosecution's position. We say that the facts are these and are inescapable: There, as I have described it, was his circle of friends, a preponderance are Muslim. During the war, there is evidence that he went out of his way to give help to Muslims, not just to those who were his friends but, on some of the evidence, to those whom he did not know. On some occasions, and this may well be a matter of common sense given the attitudes at the time, he gave that assistance when there was a direct and immediate risk to himself. At all times, there was, you may think, a general risk that he would be identified within his community as someone who was far too friendly with Muslims and who was actively helping them. The question is this: Why would he take the risk of possible death or serious repercussions in an attempt to set up, as the Prosecution suggests, some sort of mitigation for himself? You may think that he was plainly at risk of being arrested, of being investigated as a spy or collaborator, or being beaten or killed because of the help which he gave to people, and witnesses made that risk perfectly clear. After the war, he continued to give that help, not in a minor way but in a way that continued to expose him to the risks of the kind that I have set out. We say that the evidence which was presented on the defendant's behalf, evidence from those Defence witnesses about that aspect of the defendant's life, completely undermines the picture the Prosecution seek to present. The problem, we say, for the Prosecution is that their version of Goran Jelisic is simply inconsistent with the reality, and let me point to one aspect of what happened yesterday -- I'm sorry, at one point during this case. Knowing, as one did, the nature of the evidence that was going to be forthcoming, one waited with considerable interest to see how the Prosecution would counterattack the proposition that Goran Jelisic was not just a friend of Muslims but had helped many people, and how they would react to a steady procession of Muslims coming through the court, a feature which, I may say, is, I think, unique in these cases. I don't think there has been any other defendant who has been brought before this Court and been sentenced by them has had so many people from the other ethnic group, whom they have been alleged to attack, or any at all, coming and giving evidence at risk to themselves, because, of course, if they are discovered to have given evidence on behalf of, what my learned friend was pleased to call the well-known, mass killer, Goran Jelisic, you may think that they are undertaking a very considerable risk in so doing. The counterattack was quite a long time coming, but come it did. The Prosecution plainly had to find some way of explaining away what I have described as a steady procession of Muslim witnesses testifying to the good character of Goran Jelisic and to the acts of assistance he had given to them and to others, and the measure, in fact, of how weak the Prosecution's case had become on that point may be gathered from the nature of the counterattack. It came when my learned friend, Mr. Tochilovsky, was on his feet cross-examining a witness. He sought to suggest that the reason why Goran Jelisic was helping all these people was that it was somehow official policy that Muslims should be encouraged or engaged to help such people so that the Muslim population of Brcko could somehow be further reduced. Your Honours, quite frankly, quite apart from the fact that he was also trying to bolster up their appeal on genocide, Your Honours may think that to make that suggestion was simply absurd and laughable. There is simple no evidence whatever to support that proposition, and if there was, we would no doubt have heard about it a very long time ago. In any event, if that's what you were going to do, you would not need to go to the lengths of ferrying people in a small boat across the River Sava or the River Drina if the escapes had been officially sanctioned and encouraged. There are rather simpler ways of carrying out such a policy, and if there had been such a policy, as the Prosecution were trying to suggest, would it not have been somewhat transparent to those whom he aided to escape that he was not doing it out of friendship but because he was taking part in some carefully calculated policy of bloodless, ethnic cleansing? We say that that was a revealing moment in the Prosecution's case, and the Prosecution knows that the assistance which the defendant gave to Muslims during and after the war fundamentally undermines the picture which they have painted of him. The person they portray and the one that we have otherwise come to know through Defence evidence are simply not consistent, and we say -- and this is absolutely crucial -- that the Prosecution have not presented a single scrap of evidence to explain how, for a short period in May 1992, this man changes his character completely from being someone who is at ease with, draws his friends from, and assists the Muslim community to someone who spends 18 days engaged in barbaric and brutish savagery against those very same people. It simply is not consistent and is not credible. We say that the portrayal that they have placed before you is a false one. There is, of course, a reasonable, proper, and rational explanation as to why someone who was like that should engage in the kind of activities that he did, and it is self-evident from what is said about him that he is someone who is, indeed, in certain circumstances, susceptible to pressure, carrying out killings at the behest and under the pressure of others. We submit that the only rational and proper explanation as to why there should be this short, less than three week period of Goran Jelisic turning into a killer, given what you've heard about him, is that he did it not because it was his enthusiasm, not because he had suddenly turned into a racist monster, but because -- and my learned friend has, in fact, identified the reason -- there are others older and superior to him who make use of such young men, and they do it by recruiting them, placing them under the disciplines of military and police law, and making them do it. "You have to obey." We say the Prosecution recognise only too well that in that regard, Defence evidence about Goran Jelisic undermines their case. One only has to look at the explanation they've come up with to deal with the fact that as early as 1992, the defendant was saying to others what he had been doing and that he had been an unwilling participant in those events. The Prosecution's explanation goes like this: The defendant told his friends that he'd been forced to carry out the killings; the defendant fled Brcko; the defendant checked himself into a hospital and got his friends, because that's the only people who could have made these telephone calls threatening his life, got his friends to make threatening telephone calls, or perhaps he simply spoke into the receiver of the telephone when nobody was there; got himself transferred to Belgrade; imaginary telephone calls with his superiors complaining about what he had been made to do; temporarily hiding himself away in a military unit; shooting himself in the foot. All as part of a carefully, sophisticated, calculated plan to provide himself with a degree of mitigation or a defence for what he had done, just in case -- just in case -- one day someone should set up an international tribunal where he might be called to account. Again, I'm going to characterise that proposition as one which is absurd. The idea that a man of this defendant's learning and education and degree of sophistication could think up for himself, at that time and in those circumstances, such a wide-ranging and long-lasting scheme to account for his crimes in the future is, we respectfully submit, one that is absurd. Your Honour, I turn now to the issue of this defendant and how you should deal with him. The first matter is this: The defendant, having been arrested, was brought to the Tribunal. At his initial hearings, when represented by other counsel, he pleaded not guilty. Subsequently, after taking advice and considering the matter, he pleaded guilty in a way which was, with one exception, acceptable to the Prosecution. We respectfully submit that the propositions that the Prosecution has laid before you that you can safely ignore a guilty plea in his case is one which is fundamentally unfair. We say that a guilty plea is as clear an indication of remorse and, indeed, of cooperation and honesty as you could wish to have. He pleaded guilty at a very early stage; pleaded guilty, let me add, to an amended indictment. The point of that is this: There were plainly issues which had to be resolved as between Defence and Prosecution, and after proper discussions with the Prosecution, an amended indictment was produced, and when he was asked to plead to that amended indictment, he produced pleas which were acceptable -- except for Count 1, genocide -- to the Prosecution. He is now castigated for not having pleaded guilty on day 1. Your Honours, that, with great respect to my learned friend, is unfair. There were plainly matters which the Prosecution subsequently accepted, wholly defective in their initial indictment, which had to be corrected by amendment. So when that amended indictment is produced, as I say, he pleads guilty when it is first put to him. The Prosecution say that that is of no value. We respectfully invite Your Honours to say that that proposition should firmly be rejected. There is an importance in so doing. Apart from, I think, the defendant Erdemovic, Goran Jelisic is the only person to plead guilty to offences before this Tribunal. That very clearly marks him out from defendants, for example, in the Celebici trial, from Tadic, Aleksovski, Furundzija, and in the other International Tribunal, Kayishema, Ruzindena, Akayesu, who all pleaded not guilty, and there are defendants taking part in other long-standing trials, some of which have closed and are awaiting judgement, others which are ongoing. What is the effect of his plea of guilty? Whatever the Prosecution says, and even if you are to accept their proposition that it has no bearing and has no value, the reality is that the Prosecution served on the Defence the witness statements of far more people than were ever called for the genocide trial. Even if, and I do not accept it for a moment, even if you were to say the proposition that they make about witnesses not having to testify is right, the fact of the matter is that a very large number of witnesses who would have to have been called on a trial concerning the murders and other counts to which he has, in fact, pleaded guilty have not had to give evidence and relive their experiences. Secondly, there is another value to the guilty plea. It avoids any further lengthy investigation, and one knows only too well -- and it's indicated by things that have been said during this trial and other trials -- when a defendant pleads not guilty, a considerable amount of work has to be done by the Prosecution in order to bring the case ready for trial. The next matter is this, which no doubt the Prosecution would scorn because they say it's simply an indication of his trying to manipulate the Chamber: It indicates a willingness and desire to cooperate with the Chamber, and as I've indicated to you, his intention to plead guilty was indicated at a very early stage, and that is confirmed by the fact that an interview with the Office of the Prosecutor, he made, with almost embarrassing frankness, immediate admissions to offences when put to him. Your Honours can go through the interviews. You will see that there is the interviewer saying, "Now, then, we have Count so and so. It is said that you killed this man." Immediately, the defendant says, "I did" and gives an account about it. All that indicates is a consistent intention to plead guilty, to cooperate and to admit what he had done. It doesn't stand in isolation, of course, because you heard of the evidence of a witness in closed session who told you of events that took place in 1997. This was no mere flash in the pan of a defendant arriving here and being overwhelmed by the hard facts. And it's not only that. However limited the admissions that he made were, he had been admitting killings for a very long period. So the Prosecution, seeking to deny him the credit which is properly, we submit, due to someone who pleads guilty, is, in our respectful submission, ill-founded. There is also to be considered, we respectfully submit, an important public policy consideration in dealing with guilty pleas. Of course, there are some cases where despite a guilty plea a life sentence may well be appropriate, and one looks at, in recent jurisprudence of the International Tribunals, the case of Jean Kambanda, Prime Minister of his country and effectively responsible not just for all that took place in terms of his offences of genocide but responsible for his colleagues in cabinet, responsible for direction of the military and of the police. If there is anybody in the life after state who has a higher duty to protect his citizens, it is difficult to think of such a person, and the extent of the genocide in Rwanda was such that it was almost inevitable that whatever plea are tendered, whatever cooperation he gave, and it is, on the face of the judgement, substantial cooperation, inevitable that such a man would have to be sentenced to life imprisonment. Is Your Honour telling me to stop and have a break? Because I shall happily to do so if you want me to, but I was going to plough on until you told me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you think that this is a proper place to stop in your argument, I suggest that we do take a break. Do we agree?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I can happily stop there if you wish me to, certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I might ask you a question. About how long are you going to need?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Your Honour keeps on asking me that question. You will finish on time today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm asking you the question merely because I'm the Presiding Judge of this Chamber and we're trying to organise our work. Even if it was only a question of knowing whether the interpreters have to work longer than that, there's the issue of fatigue. It's not an order to constrain you in any way. I want us to be clear on that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: This is one occasion where I simply don't know how long I'm going to be. I, unlike the Prosecution, simply have some head-notes that I'm working to, and I'm trying to develop my theme on my feet, and it's not always easy to guess how long I'm going to be but I will finish in good time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. Thank you very much. That was the information I needed. Thank you, Mr. Greaves. We will take a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will now resume the hearing. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Greaves.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Your Honour, we were discussing the issue of guilty pleas and the element of encouragement that needs to be given to defendants to plead guilty, and I placed before you one example of a case where it may well be appropriate, but in highly unusual and specialised circumstances to pass a life sentence regardless of the fact that a man has pleaded guilty. But the other side of the coin is that if guilty pleas are to be encouraged, if confessions are to be encouraged, if surrenders are to be encouraged, then the surest way of discouraging them is to send out a message to defendants that, "If you plead guilty it's not going to do you a lot of good because Prosecution will castigate you for it and we'll give you a life sentence at the end of it." There is no encouragement at all sent out by the message of passing a life sentence to encourage anybody to surrender, anybody to confess, confess, anybody to plead guilty when the indictment, amended or not, is placed before him. There is, of course, another point about life sentences and whether or not it's appropriate in a case of this kind. One has to consider, in the context of this fairly specialised jurisdiction, whether or not life sentences should, in fact, be reserved for those who are guilty of the very most serious crimes. I said at the outset that I was not going so say anything which was intended to belittle the killings which this man committed and what I've just said is not intended to do that, but if there is a scale of things, then two things do occur. Firstly, it is undoubtedly the case that an offence of genocide would rank as a more serious matter than even the killings which this man has admitted. Secondly, Your Honours may consider that it would be right, as a matter of public policy, that sentences of life imprisonment should, in fact, be reserved for the people who are most culpable, most guilty, and most at the heart of what took place. I need mention no names, but there are those who have yet to be arrested or to surrender to this Tribunal to whom I am referring, because one has to mark out their conduct as being particularly serious and to mark out their behaviour as being particularly worthy of the most serious sentence. May I turn now to what is undoubtedly the thorny issue of remorse. The Prosecution are forced to rely on the evidence of somebody who has not seen the defendant for a year, and perhaps, reluctantly, you may think that Dr. Duits eventually was prepared to concede that there may have been some change, some development in the defendant, and the person best placed, whether he conducted his examination with the assistance of another psychiatrist or no, the person best placed to give you an account of that issue is Dr. Van den Bussche. I'm not going to go over at great length the evidence which we heard only yesterday, since that would be to take up time, reminding you of something which must be properly fresh in your minds, but the reality is, we submit, that there is evidence in the case, evidence which comes from a professional who deals with serial killers, is well versed with their behaviour, is sufficiently skilled, as he told you, to see through the attempts at manipulation by the defendant and to make allowance, due allowance, for those attempts when coming to his conclusions. And his evidence, you will recall, concerning remorse is evidence which we would invite you to consider and to accept, because the reality is that Dr. Duits, not having seen the defendant for a year, not being in a position to know what his present situation is, cannot properly comment on it, cannot properly gainsay that which Dr. Van den Bussche says. I move now to the issue of cooperation. I would have to accept that on the evidence that has been placed before the Tribunal, I could not properly describe that as falling -- the cooperation that he has given, I could not properly describe that as having been substantial, but simply to dismiss any cooperation as being of no value is, we respectfully submit, unfair. The fact of the matter is that he has given some assistance. The fact of the matter is, of course, that some of that material was already known to the Prosecution. And as the witness for the Prosecution conceded, it's not the defendant's fault that the Prosecution already knew that. He can only do his best in the light of what he knows. I next turn very briefly to the issue of Mr. McFadden's report, again a matter which Your Honours may feel is proper to consider, and certainly in the case of Tadic there was reference to such a report having been procured and it indicating that Tadic had behaved well whilst a prisoner. Your Honours have a similar report from Mr. McFadden, the commander of the United Nations Detention Unit -- it's dated the 25th of November 1999 -- and that indicates that, perhaps not unexpectedly, he's generally behaved reasonably well, his attitude towards the guards and management has generally been good, although there have been outbursts, mostly after verbal nature. Your Honours will of course, in the knowledge of the defendant and having had an opportunity to observe him over quite a long period of time, will understand some of the stresses that he's been through which may have led to those occasional outbursts, but they are occasional. Your Honours may think that that report demonstrates that of late he has been much better behaved, and I note from the final paragraph, sorry, the personal ultimate paragraph that Mr. McFadden's view of him at the present time is that during the last months his behaviour has been very good, and he seems to be less inclined to the erratic behaviour observed at an earlier stage of his detention. That's quite an important feature, if I may submit to Your Honours, because it may well fit in with the evidence of Dr. Van den Bussche, that this is a man who has changed and has developed particularly in recent months, and it may provide, you may feel, some support for the proposition that Dr. Van den Bussche was putting before you. Can I next turn to an issue which again the Prosecution dismisses as of peripheral or little value and that is the negotiations that the defendant undertook with a particular witness in this case. I'm not going to refer to the details of that because of the nature of the circumstances in which the witness testified, but in our respectful submission, it's important evidence for a number reasons. Firstly, it indicates a consistent pattern of how this defendant was developing towards a situation where he felt able, when placed before the Tribunal, to plead guilty and confess what he had done. Secondly, the Prosecution seek to suggest that here was a man who was simply negotiating as he wished to obtain the best possible deal. That makes, if I may say so, absolutely no allowance at all for what must be perceived as the reputation of the Tribunal amongst many of the people of Serbia and Republika Srpska. It's perhaps right to say that the Tribunal isn't the most popular institution in those two countries. I don't need to go into the reasons for that in any way, but it is a fact that the War Crimes Tribunal is not an institution that is universally admired in those parts of the world. And we heard some evidence from the witness to whom I've just referred about the concerns that the defendant had that he would be assaulted or ill-treated whilst in the United Nations Detention Unit. It's plainly not true that that would happen. Anyone who has had contact with the United Nations Detention Unit would know that fact, but reality is that in Republika Srpska and no doubt in Serbia, things are different, and anybody who was living there at that time would be prey to that propaganda, prey to those untruths and would justifiably, because they don't know what the truth is, want to express those concerns, and he wants to know, "If I surrender, am I going to be safe, because we've heard that Serbs get ill-treated by the Tribunal." Secondly, one of the defendant's concerns appears to have been, according to the witness, for his family. It's particularly cruel of the Prosecution, you may think, to think that that was simply a negotiating gambit of a man who wasn't serious of surrendering. Any human being, before he took a step of surrendering to a Tribunal in the circumstances that this man was in, would want to have some sort of reassurance whether the witness or the Tribunal was able to give it or no, would want to seek some assurance that in his absence, something might be done for his family. The Prosecution deride the defendant for having done that, in effect, saying that is simply someone trying to look after himself. In our respectful submission, that's a particularly unkind, particularly negative way to look at what the defendant was trying to do. Of course, it's easily said that if a man wants to surrender, then surrender he must and do it straightaway, but that isn't always the case in the real world, is it? Because there are some people who want to find out what's going to happen to me. "How long," as the witness told you, "how long am I going to get imprisoned? What are the conditions like? Am I," as it's been said, "going to be ill-treated if I go there? What's going to happen to my family?" Those are, in reality, perfectly proper questions for him to ask, and we respectfully submit that the evidence on this particular topic shows and has not genuinely been displaced that the defendant, realising that the game was, indeed, up and that the net was closing in around him, genuinely and sincerely made the effort to find out what would be the position if he surrendered, and held three proper meetings with a particular individual with a view to doing precisely that. No doubt, and it may be inferred from the evidence of the witness, no doubt the witness gave information to others indicating how readily available the defendant, in fact, was, and that's evident from the witness's evidence that the defendant was out and about in Bijeljina on a regular basis. So it comes as no surprise that the witness himself goes away on holiday, and very shortly after he returns home and before the defendant has had a further chance to take matters beyond that which he's already done, he's arrested and brought to The Hague. But there is, as I've indicated to Your Honours, the consistency of behaviour thereafter, which we rely on and invite Your Honours to take into consideration and say that here was a man, interested in the idea of surrendering, knowing what he was going to do when he got here, and doing precisely that; namely, confessing and pleading guilty. Your Honours are entitled to take into consideration in this case, and we invite to you do so, his age at the time of the offences and, indeed, his age now. If you were to pass upon him a life sentence, he might well live to a very old age indeed, and if it was a life sentence which you said should be a life sentence, with modern life expectancy, that might be 50, 60, or 70 years. That is an enormous amount of time. It could only be justified if there was clear and wholly unambiguous evidence that until such time as he was old and infirm he remained a danger to the public. There is no such evidence. The Prosecution, of course, try to put it the other way around: Unless you are satisfied that he isn't a danger, you should lock him up and throw the key away. That is not, in our respectful submission, the proper approach. The proper approach should be this: Three questions: Is there evidence that he is dangerous? Is there evidence that he is not dangerous? Or is there no evidence one way or the other? In our submission, there is no evidence which is proved beyond a reasonable doubt that he is dangerous and would be dangerous to the public if released. I agree equally that there is no evidence that he is not dangerous. The position is the medium position, which is there is no evidence either way, and Your Honours may think that that is the only possible conclusion to be drawn from the evidence of the doctors. If there is no evidence either way, and if it is not proved, as it has to be, beyond a reasonable doubt that he is, in fact, a danger to the public, then Your Honours must decide that issue in favour of the defendant, and I would respectfully submit, on behalf of Goran Jelisic, that there simply is no sufficient evidence to pass that test that he is dangerous. Other matters that Your Honours can consider concerning this defendant. Amongst the papers which were provided to you today is evidence which, in effect, says -- and I'll come, if I may, in a moment to the conviction in respect of dishonesty -- there is no suggestion that in his past this man has ever been guilty of any offence involving violence, any offence involving homicide, any offence involving aggressive behaviour, any offence involving racist behaviour, any offence involving public disorder. So in that sense, but in that sense alone, he comes with a completely clean slate to this Tribunal. Of course, he has the convictions that related to dishonesty and the dishonest use of cheques. I've already dealt with those, I've already made comments about them, and I don't feel the need to reemphasise those, save to say that in the context of this case, stealing or misusing cheques in a dishonest way falls into a quite different category from the kind of offences for which you have to pass sentence upon him in due course, and we respectfully submit that in the context of this case, that issue has but a peripheral importance. Next, I turn to the issue of superior orders and whether or not those were genuinely made out in this case or not. You will recall, I hope, one important piece of evidence in which a witness described how two particular individuals, Tesic and Karinovic, the inspectors, were the judge of those who were to die and those who were not to die. It's important evidence because it's quite obvious that those two individuals were heavily involved in the Luka detention facility and heavily involved in the process of deciding who it was who was to be killed, and it may well be that Your Honours accept that they were involved in deciding categories of people who were to be liquidated. Rank is an important matter, and that is obvious from all that one knows about the former Yugoslavia. Military and police ranks are serious matters, were taken seriously, and there was a clear chain of command established in these countries. These are people who are superiors to the defendant, and there is Prosecution evidence -- not Defence evidence, Prosecution evidence -- that these people were responsible for making choices and, it may be inferred from that evidence, giving orders to others, including Goran Jelisic, that individuals should be killed. We respectfully submit that the case which the Prosecution has made out in respect of this defendant being not just an enthusiastic killer but a killer who made up his own mind to kill is not made out. Let's take one example. We heard yesterday from a witness who the Prosecution called to corroborate, despite there being no requirement to do so, the evidence of another witness. The reality of the evidence of those two witnesses is this: As to important details, not as to minor and peripheral details, as to matters of important detail, the accounts given by those two witnesses are, in important detail, wholly opposed. They can't, we respectfully submit, be reconciled, the one with the other; they cannot both be true accounts. If that's right, and we respectfully submit that it is, if that is right, then ultimately it cannot be decided which of them is telling the truth, and the only proper conclusion which it would be right to draw, we submit, from those circumstances, is that the evidence as a whole should be rejected. I give but one example. Of course, the Prosecution addresses you on the basis that every one of their witnesses is absolutely truthful all of the time, and they rely on their witnesses and say, "Well, that proves this and that proves that, and that proves that the defendant was a keen and enthusiastic and willing killer." Your Honour, I'm not going to indulge this afternoon in a line-by-line examination of the evidence. What I will say is this: The Prosecution has simply ignored the fact that many of the accounts which were given by witnesses were again, as to important details, inconsistent with accounts that they had given on a previous occasion. That's important. People are invited, whether it's by courts or by the police or the security police, to give an account which they indicate, by signing their names to it, is a true account, and they do so in this case frequently at a time which was closer to the events which they were recounting, and then come to this Tribunal and give an account in respect of important matters, not peripheral matters, important matters, which is wholly in contrary distinction to the former account that was given. What is the importance of that? The previous statement is a measure by which one can judge the honesty or the reliability and accuracy of a witness, and in using those documents, it would be important and necessary to look at them and say, "Well, what have we got here? These are not differences of minor detail; these are fundamental differences which cannot for a moment be reconciled, the one with the other." The only conclusion which may properly be drawn from that level of inconsistency is either that the witness is not accurate and reliable, and if a witness is not accurate and reliable, you cannot rely upon him; or it may be worse than that, it may be that the witness is actively being untruthful, and again if the witness is being or may be being untruthful, then it would be right and, indeed, necessary to reject that evidence. The Prosecution must prove its case beyond a reasonable doubt, and producing and pointing out those inconsistencies, we submit, produces a reasonable doubt. In those circumstances, if a reasonable doubt is produced in relation to those witnesses, then it's proper and, indeed, we submit, necessary to reject the evidence. Your Honour, we went through that exercise on quite a significant number of occasions. It isn't a case of people sitting down with the security police and not having the assistance of lawyers and so on. One has to look at what it is they say, and frequently, although there is some difference sometimes between the exact wording of the statements made to the Bosnian authorities, those people sit down and say, "We confirm the truth of that which is in this statement," and frequently, one finds that there is either no reference to Goran Jelisic, or if reference is made to Goran Jelisic, it is only a very minor reference. If Goran Jelisic was the enthusiastic mass murderer that the Prosecution allege today that he is, then it would be reasonable to expect that those statements, frequently made, as they were, in late 1992 or early 1993, would confirm that position. It is a matter of some curiosity that some years later, when they come to make statements to the Prosecutor, when issues have changed somewhat, that in the statement of a particular individual and the evidence that he places before the Tribunal, Goran Jelisic is suddenly advanced to the front, he never having previously been in that witness's mind a person of great importance. That's important, and you must ask why it is, in particular, ask why it should suddenly be that a witness should change his position so radically. There is an explanation. It is because for whatever reason, and it's not for the Defence to demonstrate that reason, for whatever reason, the witness has decided to exaggerate or be untruthful about the conduct of Goran Jelisic. We respectfully remind Your Honour of all those occasions when witnesses were found to have differed in their evidence from the accounts they gave at an early stage in the early 1990s about the incidents which they had observed. Next, I turn or return somewhat to the mental condition of the defendant. I'm not going to suggest that the position is otherwise than that Goran Jelisic has some of the problems which are set out in the reports that are made and the evidence which is given about him, it would be idle to suggest otherwise, but I would respectfully remind Your Honours of, really, this: Firstly, Dr. van den Bussche indicated to you that he was able to observe and believed he had observed some progression in this man. If that is right, then, no doubt, further expertise could be brought to bear and he could receive appropriate treatment to develop that improvement. Secondly, reference is made to his conduct during the course of the trial, and again the Prosecution castigate him for it and suggest that, in some way, it is a matter which reflects badly upon him. The fact of the matter is, and this can be confirmed by, I think, Your Honours taking judicial notice of the fact, that throughout the period he has been on trial, he has been considered to be a risk of suicide, has been monitored in his cell by the prison authorities, quite properly, and there's no complaint about that. The fact of the matter is that he has been someone who has suffered from considerable anxiety and considerable stress throughout this trial, and at times, it manifests itself in a number of ways, and of course it's very irritating for us, very irritating for Your Honours, and very irritating for everyone else when he says, "I want to go out and I can't stay," of course, that's right, it is irritating, but one must make due allowance for it. Of course, comparison is made between the suffering that he's had to undergo and the suffering of his victims. It's pretty easy to make that point, but it's a cheap shot, in our submission, to make that point. The reality is that he's on trial; it is a stressful business; he was facing, until very recently, the most serious charge which can be laid against him; and, one makes no secret of it, advice that indicated that he stood firmly at risk on conviction of that crime of the longest sentence that Your Honours can pass. Well, that places any man -- any man of strong and robust constitution would be placed under stress and pressure by being tried and facing the consequences of such a conviction. So Your Honours must, in our submission, make a proper allowance to him for that. Your Honours, I want just to go through briefly some of the notes that I was able to make over the luncheon adjournment concerning the document placed before you, and I will do it quickly because my notes are fairly short and fairly quick. Paragraph 1, page 1, we respectfully submit that the proposition which is made there is not consistent with the evidence about the defendant as to his disposition prior, during, and after the war. One would agree with the first part of paragraph 2, the first four lines thereof -- and of course, it's right, he having pleaded guilty to the offences and not claimed either a special defence of diminished responsibility or duress, and he must be dealt with as if a man of full age and responsibility. That's not to say that his mental difficulties and any pressure that may have been placed on him cannot be taken into account; it plainly can be. Paragraph 3. We respectfully submit that an appeal to human instinct has no place in a court of law. It is an appeal to emotion, it is an appeal to instinct, which is not appropriate, particularly in a Tribunal composed, as Your Honour is always keen to remind me, of professional Judges. Paragraphs 5 and 6 I don't think I need comment on because they're more extensively dealt with by paragraph 7 and following. Paragraph 7 I think I've already dealt with, and I describe that as a particularly absurd suggestion, given what we know about this particular defendant. Paragraph 8. Critical comment was made of Defence witnesses who had not bothered to inquire, and it's described as "natural inquiries," taking those inquiries further about what the defendant was admitting to them. With great respect, that is a somewhat unrealistic proposition. Just imagine, Your Honours, being faced with someone you've known for many years coming to you and saying, "I've committed a whole lot of murders." Short of someone saying to you, "My husband," or, "My wife has just died," it is perhaps no more difficult a thing to think of an answer to or about which you would want to make inquiries. It's probably the most difficult thing to try to deal with. And just imagine the conversation you would have with somebody who came to you with such a confession. It's perhaps unsurprising that the people that you saw, considerably less sophisticated than most of us in this court, found it difficult to deal with that proposition, not least those who were aware of rumours that the defendant was killing Muslims and who were themselves Muslims. They must have found that an extremely difficult time, and it is perhaps unsurprising that they felt unable to make further inquiries. There is a second aspect, of course, and one which perhaps doesn't immediately occur to us, but just remember what the atmosphere was in that part of the world at that time. Knowledge was dangerous. If somebody knew that you knew he'd been involved in killings or ordering killings, they would have a significant motive for doing harm to you. So asking too many questions was not a very smart idea. You would put yourself in a position where you would have knowledge which others might seek to prevent you dissipating or disclosing to others. Paragraph 9 I think I've already dealt with largely. We respectfully submit that that is not a proper approach for Your Honours to take. At paragraph 10, it's inevitable that amongst some of the circle of friends of the defendant that some of them won't know the intimate details of what goes on in his household. Of course that's right and it's obvious. To castigate witnesses and to say that their evidence is of less value because they didn't know that is, we respectfully submit, not a good point. The Prosecution again castigates those who were close friends who were uninformed about his behaviour. One can make this comment: It's not exactly the sort of thing that you tell your best friends if they themselves are ordinary, decent people. Of course, there was one who pointed out what he had done with it, but in large part, we say that it's unlikely that he would come along and say, "Well, by the way, you know that nice new car I've got and the dinner we had the other night? Well, that was the proceeds of crime." That's not a realistic approach, we submit. Witness DR, paragraph 12, misrepresents, we submit, her evidence. What she says is this, it's two things: First of all, was it simply a question of her child going off with a complete stranger on its own, but there was evidence from her that another child went with him; but secondly, she told you this: "The suggestion was made to make the child on holiday. The defendant went away and came back a week later. During which time I had time to think about the proposition. And one may conclude, think about the defendant, and having thought about him, I concluded that this was a safe and proper thing to do ." She's Muslim. She has come here at risk to herself. If anybody finds out that she's given evidence on behalf of the defendant, she is placing herself at risk. Would she do that if, firstly, this was untrue; and secondly, if there had been some improper motive behind what she had done? We submit that the motives ascribed to her were ones which were unworthy motives. Paragraph 13. The Prosecution inevitably, when it has the opportunity to benefit from hearsay evidence, is content to invite Your Honours to rely upon it. When the Defence produces hearsay evidence, which of course is admissible before this Tribunal, where evidence is produced for which a proper foundation is laid -- and by that I mean a proper foundation as was envisaged by the very early decision before this Tribunal made in the Tadic case concerning the admissibility of hearsay evidence -- where a proper foundation is laid, the Prosecution, regardless of that, says that it must be ignored. Well, I would invite Your Honours to say, as you've indicated quite clearly during the trial, hearsay evidence is admissible. It's effectively a matter for Your Honours to decide. Firstly, is the evidence reliable, and if it's reliable, what weight should we give to it? The fact of the matter is that a large number of Defence witnesses came along and said, "This is what we've heard." Of course, the Prosecution called a large number of witnesses who also gave hearsay evidence, evidence that plainly came from people who are still alive and well. So the same criticism can be made, and I think in particular of the lists which we went through at some length of time, the same criticism can be made of the Prosecution's approach. Well, if it's okay for them, it ought to be okay for us to produce hearsay evidence. Your Honours, it is evidence and you are obliged to consider it. You may reject it if you wish, but if it is well founded, if it is reliable, then you can take it into account. Paragraph 15. This, of course, is the second way in which the Prosecution seeks to deal with the uncomfortable facts of the number of people, Muslim, who were helped by the defendant. The second string that they seek to fit to their bow is, "Oh, well, this is the defendant acting out some hero role." Doesn't do it out of real remorse or guilt, but simply to polish, as they say, his own ego. Might he have done it out of friendship? After all, many of those whom he helped were his friends from before the war. They ascribe, on every occasion, the worst possible motive to an act of friendship. Your Honours, I don't need to go through the detail of the number of people who said, "This defendant helped me, at risk to himself. This defendant helped members of my family, at risk to himself, and it's within my knowledge that he helped others who were not his friends." Is that simply polishing of ego or is it someone acting out of friendship, friendships which he had formed a long time ago, and acting quite properly? Of course, it may be in part that he felt the need to do it in the light of what he had done and to try hard to put things right. That may be one part of it. But simply to say, "Oh, well, it's polishing his ego," is simply far too facile, we respectfully submit. Paragraph 16. The Prosecution complain that Defence witnesses do not deal with his behaviour after the war. Again, we respectfully submit that that is to misrepresent the evidence. One only has to think, for example, of the witness who described how large numbers of his family were helped by the defendant to escape from his home area after the war, when he eventually went off, I think it was, to one of the countries in Europe. So simply to say there isn't any evidence or almost none of it dealt with his behaviour after the war is simply not correct. And he wasn't the only one. The Prosecution seeks to make something out, although it's not clear what they're trying to make it out of the absence of any indication as to what he did in the years up to his arrest in 1998. There isn't any evidence about it and it would be wrong to draw conclusions one way or another. I have dealt with the issue of his thinking of surrendering. There is no evidence to support the suggestion at all that he was being supervised by people in the town, and we would respectfully invite you to reject that contention. I've already told Your Honours that the evidence shows that it was engaged in meaningful and realistic negotiations about surrender. Paragraph 19. An assertion is made with the order "maybe" put in front of it, someone having money to give -- "the defendant having money to give away (maybe from the smuggling of cars or other black-market activities)." No evidence of that at all. The defendant plainly did have access to a false identification document, and you will remember that there was evidence that he helped some Muslims to obtain false identity documents, and so again Your Honours may think that that's not the best point that the Prosecution have to make in this case. Finally in that paragraph, the Prosecution say that this is all evidence that he was not in danger of being liquidated by the authorities. That may be a proper conclusion to draw but, of course, the instant danger had long since passed. The real time of stress and anxiety that something might happen to him would have been back in 1992 and 1993, when these matters were still fresh and people were still concerned that he was a potentially loose cannon who might go off and start disclosing uncomfortable facts to other people. It may well be that in time things had got easier. "Confessions in interview." If I may turn to paragraph 22, please. The defendant is castigated for his refusal to allow his mind to be explored in relation to genocide. I'm puzzled by that. I would have thought it obvious from everything that's happened in this case that the defendant has never accepted being guilty of genocide. He's been acquitted of that, and the rules say quite clearly that a defendant is entitled not to say anything about it if he so chooses. If he said nothing about his state of mind as to genocide, he was doing not more than exercising that which is his right guaranteed to him under Articles 20 and 21 in the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. So I would respectfully invite Your Honours to reject that remark as being wholly out of place. I've dealt with the issue of cooperation. I accept that the defendant didn't, in fact, surrender himself voluntarily, but I have made observations about that matter. Comment is made at page 9, paragraph 23(d), about the defendant limiting matters which he was willing to talk about. There may be all sorts of reason for that, and some might be unworthy, some might be worthy. For example, it may be that a defendant is particularly sensitive about a particular individual who he's not prepared to talk about because that person presents a particular risk to him. Who knows. It's not a factor, I respectfully submit, that ought to be taken into consideration. Paragraphs 26 and 27 I've dealt with at some length, the issue of guilty pleas which are tendered by a defendant, and I won't go back across that ground, save and expect, at paragraph 30, the observation that was made by my learned friend that he admitted very little beyond what the evidence established. Of course, that may be that what the evidence established was no more than that which had happened. He's also criticised again in that paragraph for avoiding answering that which was crucial and difficult. Again, it's well within his rights, if he so chooses, not to answer the questions. Again, a right guaranteed to him. And Your Honours should not speculate on his motives for so doing because it would be wrong, we submit, to do so. He's castigated again for his plea of guilty not being of any particular value to national reconciliation. Well, that's a matter entirely for Your Honours to judge. Of course, he falls into a different category from, for example, a Jean Kambanda. He's not a prime minister; he's not a cabinet minister; he's not a member of a war presidency; he's not a local councillor; he's not a General in the army, but he is someone who took part in terrible events in a sensitive place, and his willingness to plead guilty ought to be held up as an example to others. If it's held up as an example to others, in the way that I suggested, by Your Honours giving encouragement to others, if others come forward as a result of seeing that you get credit from a plea of guilty and that a plea of guilty is treated well, then that very process will aid national reconciliation if other defendants, seeing what Your Honours do, recognise that there is, in fact, not only mercy but a sensible policy of encouraging pleas of guilty. They may, thereby, be encouraged to surrender. If that happens, then one of the by-products of that is or may be a degree of assistance to the national reconciliation process. I've dealt with the issue of his conduct at the trial. I'm not going to go over it again. If I may turn to page 16 in the English version, Your Honours, issue of superior orders. Of course there may be cases where the fact that someone is at the very bottom of the chain of command, if I can put it that way, or at the very bottom, in other words, as a private soldier or an ordinary policeman, doesn't necessarily prevent them from being given long or maximum sentences. Each case, of course, has to be treated on its merits and on its own facts, and the cases which are set out in some considerable detail with all their references there, Your Honours may feel perhaps not entirely on the same level as the ones which we are dealing with here today. Paragraph 40. The suggestion is made that he was hiding from investigators -- sorry -- there may have been things he wished to hide from investigators and experts. The Prosecution say it's unclear what he did. No evidence to support that proposition. Paragraph 49, discriminatory behaviour. Of course, as a proposition, the existence of a racial motive or racist motive to a crime, in many jurisdictions, is one that can serve to aggravate it, and that, in this modern world of ours, is one proposition which is well accepted pretty well everywhere. I don't dissent from that as a proposition. As far as the conduct of the defendant is concerned, I have already and at some length arrested Your Honours as to what we say is the unreliability of the Prosecution's witnesses, and that it's not accepted that that's what he did, and it does not fit with the Goran Jelisic who was the friend of Muslims and helped Muslims as a consistent matter. And that, we say, is a proper basis for you to reject that proposition and say that it's one that needn't be taken into account in this case. Again, paragraph 52, we have this business of the defendant setting up witnesses and that being proposed as an aggravating circumstance. Well, if Your Honours think that all those witnesses were dupes who came along because they had been manipulated in some way by the defendant, then of course you might wish to follow that proposition. But we respectfully submit that simple though they may have been, misjudged the defendant they may have, these were ordinary, decent people who knew the defendant, who said, "Well, that's what I knew about him. That's how I knew him. What can I say? I got it wrong. Plainly there was something about him that I did not know, but what I can tell you, and that's all I can tell you, is he was a friend of Muslims. He assisted Muslims." That's the bare bones of what they say. Were they being dishonest about that or trying to pull the wool over Your Honours' eyes? Would they take the risk of coming here to try and assist pulling the wool over Your Honours' eyes, knowing that if they're found out then the risk to be them is great. In our respectful submission, although many witnesses take a risk by coming here, and I accept the Prosecution witnesses take a risk, the risk that a Muslim living anywhere near Brcko or Bijeljina or in the federation takes by giving evidence on behalf of what the Prosecution is pleased to call the mass killer, Jelisic, is infinitely greater. Just imagine how popular someone would be amongst his Muslim community if he was found to have been giving comfort and succour to the defendant Goran Jelisic. One could well imagine that he would be at real risk for having done that. We submit that the suggestion that those people were manipulated and set up is simply without substance. Next, I turn to gravity of the offence. Of course, and everything, I hope, that I have said indicates that we accept this, the taking of human life is a most grave matter, it's always a grave matter, and it always has serious and grave consequences for other members of the family, for the friends, and for the community in which those people live. In those senses, Goran Jelisic has to answer for those grave offences, and he knows that and accepts that and has been for some time accepting of that proposition. What one must still do, and the exercise that one still must carry out, we submit, is consider carefully whether or not it's really made out that this defendant changed, in a period of 18 days, from an ordinary young man with a bit of a past into the blood-thirsty killer that the Prosecution would have you believe, or not. If there is doubt about that, and we submit that there is, then a proper case can be made for a much lesser sentence than that which the Prosecution asserts is appropriate in such strong terms. We submit that that's a proper course for you to follow in this case. Paragraph 54. I revisited the most recent Tadic decision on sentence last night and was interested to discover that, yes, there is a difference quantitatively between war crimes and crimes against humanity. In respect to the second decision on sentence that was passed, I think, only about ten days ago, on the counts which involved war crimes, which were deemed to be lesser in seriousness than crimes against humanity, the sentence was one of 24 years; crimes against humanity, the sentence was one of 25 years. My primitive mathematics reveal that that is a four per cent difference being considered appropriate between war crimes and crimes against humanity, and so if there is a distinction, it is a pretty small one, in the opinion of that Trial Chamber. I would invite Your Honours to look at very carefully the dissenting judgement of Judge Robinson in that case. We would adopt that dissenting judgement. It makes out a clear case, we submit, as to why the proposition that there is a useful distinction to be drawn between crimes against humanity and war crimes, that that distinction, if it exists, is a wholly artificial one or that, in fact, in reality doesn't exist at all. If you think about it, look for a moment at the way in which people are indicted before this Tribunal, it is habitually the case that people are indicted for the three different forms of committing an offence: a crime against humanity, a grave breach of the Geneva Convention, or as a violation of the laws or customs of war. But the crime which is being alleged against the defendant, the act which is sought to make the defendant guilty, the act is the same one, it's the same killing, and it is, with great respect, a wholly artificial thing to do, to sentence somebody on the basis of labels which you put on crimes. We submit that the proper approach is to sentence somebody for what he has done, not for the label which you put upon it, because doing that is, as I've described it, an artificial exercise.
