The artificiality of it was, in reality, recognised by the Judges in the most recent Tadic decision, by making a distinction only of four per cent, one year, between the sentence for crimes against humanity and war crimes. So it may well be that we can proceed on the basis that that particular artificial distinction is now going to become a matter of history. Paragraph 56. It is a matter of regret that the word "extermination" should appear there and somehow be attributed -- or the defendant should somehow be added into that proposition. He has been acquitted of genocide and he's not charged with persecution, and so it's wrong that you should consider this to be part of a wider pattern of extermination if he is not charged any more than either of those two offences. Paragraph 57. I've dealt with the issue of danger. Paragraph 63 is the next one which I want to address Your Honours about, and in a moment, I shall find some notes that I have. I have no problem with the propositions that are made out as far as the general practice regarding prison sentences in the courts of the former Yugoslavia. Such practice may be used as guidance and is not binding on the Trial Chamber. That is plainly the jurisprudence of the day. I hope that I can assist Your Honours by giving you a little bit more assistance with the sentencing practice for war crimes in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I have been able to find some details of four cases. I don't have the actual law reports in relation to them because I've been reliant on a colleague in Sarajevo recently sending to me information about these matters, but I can tell Your Honours about four matters. In, I think, 1995, a youth called Dragan Opacic was convicted of war crimes against the civilian population under Article 142 of the Criminal Code of the SFRY, which was then still the law of Bosnia-Herzegovina. He was convicted of 23 murders committed with firearms, two other homicides, ten rapes, and for offences involving mistreatment of prisoners, he having been one of the guards in the Keraterm camp. He was sentenced to ten years in a juvenile prison. That is the maximum punishment, as I understand it, which could be imposed on a person of his age, and that explains the sentence of ten years, and I believe that he was between the age of 16 and 18 at the time of sentence. The second case involved somebody called Veselin Cancar. I'm sorry. I've got a judgement number for that if you want to get further information about it. The judgement number has been given to me as KM-11/95. Veselin Cancar, which is judgement number K-186/96, he was convicted of war crimes against the civilian population, again Article 142. He had been camp commander at Foca. He was found guilty of illegal detention, for the physical and psychological mistreatment of detainees, guilty of one murder and tortures that caused grievous bodily harm to more persons. He was initially sentenced to 11 years, but on appeal, the supreme court reduced that to nine years. The next case is Milan Hrvacevic, K-122/96 is the judgement number; again Article 142 of the Criminal Code of the SFRY. Convicted of war crimes; intentional devastation of a civilian installation of great scope and value, one million Deutschemarks; endangering lives of civilians in them; convicted and sentenced to 15 years; on appeal, sentence reduced to 12 years. It may be that one thinks that that's perhaps not entirely similar to our present circumstances here. The final case is judgement number K-14/93. Borislav Herak and Svetko Damjanovic, they were convicted of genocide under Article 141, war crimes against civilians under Article 142, and war crimes against prisoners of war under Article 144 of the Criminal Code of SFRY. Herak had killed 40 civilians. He was initially sentenced to death, but subsequently, after appeals, that was reduced to 20 years. My informant seems to have missed out telling us what happened to the other defendant, but it may have been that that wasn't a similar set of circumstances. So there I've set out a number of judgements. My learned friend made the observation about consistency of sentencing, and it's one which I would, in general, endorse, but to this extent: There should be consistency of sentencing not just before this Tribunal, but because it involves the former Yugoslavia, there should be some degree of consistency with the sentencing that is taking place arising out of this conflict in the former Yugoslavia. If the situation were to arise that a wholly different set of tariffs was to be practised here compared with sentences being passed in the former Yugoslavia, then that would raise the suggestion of some degree of unfairness. If one comes here and you get longer sentences, it may be thought to be better to surrender yourself to Sarajevo and get convicted there, if possible. So, yes, there should be consistency, but it should be consistency across the board, not just consistency between sentences at the International Tribunal or international tribunals. I'm conscious of the time, Your Honours. I'm coming, I hope, as rapidly as I may, towards an end. In the context of consistency of sentencing, I'm not going to take Your Honours through, in any detail, the various decisions that have been made by this Tribunal in relation to sentence. Those are matters that you can look at in the comfort of the deliberation Chamber, if I may call it that, and Your Honours are fully familiar with it. Some of Your Honours have been involved in some of the sentencing decisions in any event, and it would be idle of me to lecture you about them. But if one looks carefully at each of the set of facts in each of the different cases that one has, there is, as my learned friend indicates, beginning to be a degree of jurisprudence that one can see as to the level of sentencing that has taken place. It may be helpful, of course, to remind Your Honours of some of the other cases that do not relate to this Tribunal. There have been a number of decisions before the Rwanda Tribunal, perhaps more apposite because each of the cases before the Rwanda Tribunal involves, in general, genocide, persecution, crimes against humanity, down to war crimes simpliciter as well. I've reminded you of some of the facts concerning Jean Kambanda, and that, perhaps I've indicated to Your Honours, is a case that falls into a class of its own, and perhaps Your Honours may feel and would agree that it can't be used as a particularly helpful guideline in this case. The case of Kayishema and Ruzindena. Kayishema, a fully contested trial, convicted of four counts of genocide, including by way of being responsible as a superior as prefect of Kabayu [phoen] in Rwanda. He received a sentence of life imprisonment, and one knows only too well that the facts of the genocide in that case, as indeed in pretty well every case before the Rwanda Tribunal, involves responsibility for killings on an extremely wide scale. By contrast, the codefendant in that trial, Ruzindena, again fully contested trial, no plea of guilty, convicted of one count of genocide. In very brief terms, the case against him was that he had orchestrated and directed killings in the thousands of Tutsis, and he had personal involvement in at least one killing. Remember this: Fully contested trial; sentence, 25 years. Akayesu, convicted of a wide range of offences, extermination, genocide, incitement of genocide, murder as a crime against humanity, torture, rape, inhumane acts. Fully contested trial. He had been the burgermeister of his particular commune and, according to the judgement, personally participated in at least 16 murders; life imprisonment. Then I turn finally to the case of Serushago. Can I commend to Your Honours the case of Serushago, which sets out in an extremely concise form not just some of the jurisprudence involving sentencing but the facts and the aggravating and mitigating features that were both present in that case and are ones which -- one saw my learned friend using, as it were, the headlines as items to consider, it's a decision which I commend to Your Honours. The defendant in that case surrendered himself, pleaded guilty, pleaded to genocide, murder, extermination, and torture, as I say, pleaded guilty. There was plainly considerable cooperation in that case by that defendant. So if one looks at trying to balance it in a non-artificial way, on the one hand, he pleads guilty to offences which are, on the face of it, more serious than even simple killings, to wit, genocide and extermination; the balancing factor in his case is one where he gives significant cooperation to the prosecution in that case. Given all those circumstances, and remember, as I indicated to Your Honours, that genocide in Rwanda is the real thing, we're talking about hundreds of thousands of people, 15 years was the appropriate sentence in that case. Now, I pick those out. It's not our intention to invite Your Honours -- to say to Your Honours, "We think that 'X' years is appropriate in this case." I'm not going to do that, firstly, because we don't think it's appropriate that the Defence should advocate a particular sentence to be passed upon the defendant, save and except that the only sentence that's available to you is one of imprisonment, but we're not going to invite you to say -- to recommend to Your Honours a particular figure; secondly, because it has the practical problem of if we did it, we would be giving a hostage to fortune as far as any right on appeal will be concerned, and it's for that reason that we don't consider it appropriate to make any recommendation to Your Honours. What we do do, and what I hope has been clear that I've been trying to do, is to point Your Honours to some of the jurisprudence that is, perhaps, rather more up to date than the Nuremberg cases which upon the Prosecution relies, pointing Your Honours to some of those cases and saying, "Let's begin to look at the element of uniformity, the element of consistency that is developing amongst the two Tribunals that are charged with the task of trying those guilty of serious offences against international humanitarian law." Your Honour, I conclude by saying this: I've indicated that we do not wish, and it's certainly not our intention, to belittle in any way those offences which the defendant committed. He knows that they are grave and he knows that a substantial sentence must follow for those killings, and he is accepting of that. I can say that to Your Honour. I don't wish to give evidence, but it's quite plain, from all that he has said, that he does accept that it's not going to be a short sentence, nor do we suggest that a short sentence is, in any sense, appropriate. But all the facts and all the features that I've urged upon you are ones that I invite Your Honours to accept, invite Your Honours to follow, and however terrible the crimes were -- and one only has to look at the series of photographs that were produced to understand that they are terrible crimes -- however terrible they were, the reasons do not exist to take the rest of this man's freedom away for the rest of what may be a long life, and that the proper approach is that which I recommended to Your Honours, to look at other jurisprudence, other cases, and to fit this case into the scale of those cases, taking into account all the factors, and pass a sentence which gives him some light at the end of the tunnel and does not crush the human spirit. Those are my submissions on behalf of Goran Jelisic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to thank Mr. Greaves. I think neither the Prosecution, nor the Defence feels that this Trial Chamber prevented them from fully developing their arguments. I will now say that the proceedings are completed in the trial of Goran Jelisic and tell you that the sentence, at least the decision, will be rendered between the 10th and the 15th of December, 1999. The court stands adjourned.
